column3: Fun Fact
The Common Mormon’s entire life cycle, from egg-laying to the death of the adult, can last about 30 to 43 days.
Common Mormon eggs usually hatch after only 3 to 5 days.
Common Mormon caterpillars pass through five growth stages, called instars, before becoming pupae.
Young Common Mormon caterpillars have white markings that make them look like bird droppings, helping camouflage them from predators.
When threatened, a Common Mormon caterpillar can push out a forked organ called an osmeterium that releases unpleasant chemicals to discourage predators.
Some female Common Mormons mimic butterflies that predators find unpleasant to eat, such as the Common Rose and Crimson Rose.
This protective trick is called Batesian mimicry: the edible Common Mormon copies butterflies that predators avoid.
Some female Common Mormons copy both the look and the flying style of butterflies that predators avoid.
Male Common Mormons gather minerals from moist ground and other damp places through a behaviour called puddling
Minerals collected by males during puddling can later be transferred to females during mating and can improve egg-hatching success.
A Tailed Jay can develop from an egg into an adult butterfly in about 33–36 days.
Tailed Jay eggs are laid one at a time on young leaves and usually hatch after only 3–4 days.
After hatching, a young Tailed Jay caterpillar usually eats its own empty eggshell as its first meal.
Tailed Jay caterpillars go through five growth stages, called instars, over about 15–16 days.
Between feeding periods, Tailed Jay caterpillars often rest along the middle vein of a leaf.
When disturbed, a Tailed Jay caterpillar can push out a hidden, forked organ called an osmeterium, which releases a smelly secretion to help discourage predators.
Before becoming a pupa, the caterpillar prepares a silk pad and a silk “belt” called a girdle to help hold itself in place.
The Tailed Jay’s pupal stage lasts about 12–13 days, and just before the adult emerges, its green wing spots can become visible through the pupal skin.
Tailed Jays develop so quickly that there can be seven or eight generations in one year
Tailed Jays are strong and restless fliers and may keep fluttering their wings even while visiting flowers.
Oriental Pied Hornbills can make crow-like calls, braying sounds, harsh crackles and screeches.
Oriental Pied Hornbills usually form one breeding pair rather than having several mates at the same time.
They usually do not dig their own nest holes. Instead, they use existing cavities in trees.
After entering a nest cavity, the female seals most of the entrance using materials such as mud, plant material and other natural materials.
The female leaves only a narrow opening in the sealed nest so food can still be passed inside.
While the female is sealed inside the nest, the male collects food and passes it to her through the small opening.
After the chicks hatch, the female feeds them with food brought to the nest by the male.
The female and chicks can remain inside the nest cavity for several months before the young birds are ready to leave.
Oriental Pied Hornbills may return to the same nest they used in an earlier breeding season.
Their breeding season can begin around February, and its timing can coincide with the beginning of the rainy season and greater fruit availability, depending on location.
The orange and red colour on a Rhinoceros Hornbill’s bill and casque comes from oil that the bird rubs onto them from a gland near its tail.
Rhinoceros Hornbills can make a loud two-part call that can be heard from several kilometres away, and pairs may call together as a duet.
Their wings make a loud whooshing sound when they fly.
During nesting, the female stays inside a tree cavity with the eggs and chicks while the male brings food to the nest.
The pair seals most of the nest entrance with a mixture that can include mud, food and droppings.
They leave only a tiny opening in the sealed nest, just large enough for the male to pass food inside and for waste to be pushed out.
When the chicks are fully feathered and old enough to leave, the parents chip away the dried nest seal to open the cavity.
The female must rely heavily on her mate during nesting, so courtship and pair bonding are especially important before she seals herself inside the nest.
Rhinoceros Hornbills are the national bird of Malaysia and the state bird of Sarawak.
The Rhinoceros Hornbill’s name comes from its large horn-shaped casque, which resembles the horn of a rhinoceros.
The Asian Elephant is the largest living land animal in Asia.
Evidence suggests Asian elephants typically live into their mid-50s, although their lifespan in the wild is not fully understood.
An adult Asian elephant can eat up to about 150 kilograms of food in a day.
Asian elephants have one finger-like tip at the end of their trunk, which helps them handle small objects precisely.
An Asian elephant’s trunk can hold about 7.6 litres of water and is used for drinking, smelling, touching, lifting and communicating.
Asian elephants can communicate over long distances using very low-pitched rumbles that other elephants can hear from more than 2 miles away.
Elephants can use smell to recognise another elephant’s identity, sex and reproductive condition.
Asian elephants often touch one another with their trunks to communicate greetings, reassurance, play and other social messages.
Asian elephants grow six sets of teeth during their lives, and new teeth move forward to replace worn ones like a conveyor belt.
Asian elephants can use tools and show behaviours associated with grief and compassion.
The Malayan Tiger is the national animal of Malaysia.
A Malayan Tiger can live for up to about 20 years in the wild.
Malayan Tigers are smaller on average than Bengal Tigers.
Their orange coat and dark stripes help them blend into the background while stalking prey.
Malayan Tigers are excellent swimmers and are known to enjoy being in water.
Malayan Tigers are usually solitary, except during mating or when mothers are nurturing the cubs.
Female Malayan Tigers can leave scent signals to show males that they are ready to mate, while males use scent to mark their territory.
Malayan Tigers can communicate using different sounds, including chuffs, moans, growls and roars.
Tiger cubs are born blind; their eyes begin to open after about 6–12 days and they gain full vision at around two weeks old.
Malayan Tiger cubs usually stay with their mother until they are about two years old before leaving to live independently.
The Malayan Tapir is the largest of the world’s tapir species.
Average lifespan of Malayan tapirs is approximately 30 years. They have been recorded living up to 36.5 years in captivity.
Baby Malayan Tapirs are born with pale stripes and spots, but these markings gradually fade by about six months of age.
A Malayan Tapir has a flexible snout formed by its nose and upper lip, which it can use to grasp leaves and bring food to its mouth.
Malayan Tapirs are good swimmers and can even walk along the bottom of deep rivers while holding their breath for up to about 90 seconds.
They are most active during the evening and night, especially around dusk and dawn.
Malayan Tapirs can communicate using whistles, clicks and hiccup-like sounds.
A Malayan Tapir pregnancy lasts about 13 to 13.5 months, and usually only one calf is born at a time.
A newborn Malayan Tapir can usually stand within one or two hours after birth and can swim when it is only about three weeks old.
If a predator attacks, a Malayan Tapir may escape into water. If the attacker grabs its neck, it may try to knock it off against a tree.
The Sun Bear is the smallest bear species in the world.
Sun Bears have extremely long tongues that help them reach honey hidden inside bee nests.
The pale patch on a Sun Bear’s chest gives the species its name because it can resemble a rising sun.
A Sun Bear’s chest patch can be U-shaped, round or shaped like a spot. Some Sun Bears have no chest patch at all!
Sun Bears are excellent climbers and are considered the most tree-dwelling of all bear species.
They can build sleeping platforms high in trees using branches and leaves.
Unlike many bears, Sun Bears do not hibernate because food is available throughout the year in their tropical environment.
Sun Bears can mate throughout the year instead of having only one short breeding season.
A mother Sun Bear usually gives birth to one or two cubs, and the cubs remain with their mother for years while they grow.
Mother Sun Bears have been observed carrying a cub in their arms while walking on their hind legs, an unusual behaviour among bears.
In the wild, Proboscis Monkeys are found only on the island of Borneo.
Proboscis Monkeys can swim across rivers and may even swim underwater for up to about 20 metres.
Their partially webbed fingers and toes help them move through water.
Adult males have very large noses that can help make their calls louder.
A male’s large nose may help attract females and intimidate rival males by amplifying his calls.
Proboscis Monkeys usually live in groups with one adult male, several females and their young.
Several Proboscis Monkey groups may gather together near water at night to sleep.
Male Proboscis Monkeys make different calls for different situations, including honks for group communication and alarm calls when danger is nearby.
Young Proboscis Monkeys begin eating solid food at about six weeks old and are usually weaned at around seven months.
A mother Proboscis Monkey may allow other members of her group to hold her baby.
The Lesser Mouse-deer is one of the smallest hoofed mammals in the world and can weigh only around 1.4–2.5 kg.
Unlike true deer, Lesser Mouse-deer do not have antlers or horns. Adult males instead have protruding canine teeth.
Male Lesser Mouse-deer have a swollen scent gland beneath the chin that is used in territorial marking and reproductive behaviour.
Lesser Mouse-deer are mainly active around dawn and dusk, although some may also be active at night.
Researchers once thought Lesser Mouse-deer were mainly nocturnal, but later studies found that they can also be active during the daytime.
Female Lesser Mouse-deer can reproduce throughout the year instead of having only one breeding season.
Males use their elongated canine teeth in fights with other males.
Lesser Mouse-deer are usually solitary or live in pairs rather than forming large herds.
The Lesser Mouse-deer has a distinctive inverted V-shaped, or chevron, white marking on its throat and upper chest.
The mouse-deer, known as “Sang Kancil” in Malay folklore, is famous as a clever trickster character in traditional stories.
The Sunda Colugo is also called the Sunda Flying Lemur, but it is not actually a lemur and it does not truly fly.
A large skin membrane called a patagium stretches from the neck to the limbs, fingers, toes and tail, allowing the colugo to glide between trees.
A Sunda Colugo can glide for more than 100 metres while losing very little height.
Longer glides can actually give a Sunda Colugo a softer landing because it can slow itself down in the air before reaching a tree.
Sunda Colugos are excellent climbers in trees but are very awkward and almost helpless on the ground.
They are mainly active at night, and their large eyes help them see well in dim light.
A mother Sunda Colugo carries her baby clinging underneath her body, even while she is gliding.
A mother can fold part of her gliding membrane near her tail to make a warm pouch-like shelter for her baby.
A Sunda Colugo pregnancy lasts about 60 days, and usually one baby is born at a time, although twins are rare.
When threatened, a Sunda Colugo may climb higher into a tree or stay completely still instead of trying to fight.
The Malayan Pangolin is also known as the Sunda Pangolin.
A Malayan Pangolin has no teeth and uses a very long sticky tongue to collect ants and termites.
Its tongue can extend to about 25 cm and is so long that part of it passes through the chest and anchors near the pelvis.
Malayan Pangolins are covered in overlapping scales made from keratin, the same material found in human hair and nails.
When threatened, a mother pangolin can curl into a tight ball with her baby protected inside.
A young Malayan Pangolin can ride on the base of its mother’s tail while travelling.
Malayan Pangolins are mainly nocturnal and usually live alone, although they are sometimes seen in pairs.
They can climb trees using their strong claws and prehensile tail, and they have also been observed swimming.
A Malayan Pangolin can close its nostrils and ear openings, which helps protect them while digging into ant or termite nests.
Newborn Malayan Pangolins have soft scales that harden after birth, and usually only one young is born at a time.
Green Sea Turtles get their name from the greenish colour of their body fat, not from the colour of their shell.
Green Sea Turtles can live for at least 70 years or more.
Adult Green Sea Turtles are the only sea turtles whose diet is mainly herbivorous, feeding mostly on seagrass and algae.
Female Green Sea Turtles are remarkable navigators and usually return to a beach in the same general area where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
Green Sea Turtles can migrate hundreds to thousands of miles between feeding areas and nesting beaches.
Green Sea Turtles can travel very long distances between their feeding grounds and nesting beaches, sometimes crossing entire ocean regions.
A female Green Sea Turtle can lay around 100–200 eggs in a single nest, then cover the nest and return to the sea.
Green Sea Turtle eggs incubate in warm sand for about two months before the hatchlings emerge.
Newly hatched Green Sea Turtles find the ocean by moving toward the brightest horizon and away from the dark outline of dunes and vegetation.
The temperature of the sand around a sea turtle nest can influence whether the hatchlings develop as males or females.
The Reticulated Python is the longest snake species in the world.
Its name “reticulated” comes from the net-like pattern on its skin.
Reticulated Pythons are non-venomous and kill prey by constriction.
Heat-sensitive pits around the lips help a Reticulated Python detect warm-blooded prey.
Reticulated Pythons rely heavily on smell and touch because they do not hear airborne sounds the way humans do.
Instead of external ears, they can sense vibrations travelling through the ground.
Reticulated Pythons are excellent swimmers and have even been recorded far out at sea.
A female can lay a large clutch of eggs; NParks reports around 15–80 eggs in a clutch.
Reticulated Python eggs can take about 88 days to hatch.
Male Reticulated Pythons may fight other males when competing for a female.
The Saltwater Crocodile is the largest living reptile in the world.
Saltwater Crocodiles can live for about 70 years in the wild.
Saltwater Crocodiles are excellent swimmers and can travel long distances through the sea.
They are ambush predators that can stay almost motionless before suddenly attacking prey near the water’s edge.
Their eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on the head, allowing most of the body to remain hidden underwater while they watch and breathe.
Saltwater Crocodiles have special pressure-sensitive organs around their jaws that help them detect movements and vibrations in the water.
Female Saltwater Crocodiles build mound-shaped nests from vegetation and mud and lay their eggs inside.
The temperature inside a crocodile nest helps determine whether the hatchlings develop as males or females.
A mother Saltwater Crocodile can help newly hatched babies reach the water by gently carrying them in her mouth.
Saltwater Crocodiles use their powerful tails as the main source of thrust when swimming.
Yellow-bellied Bulbuls are resident birds, meaning they usually stay in the same general region all year instead of making long seasonal migrations.
They are mainly forest birds and often stay hidden in dense vegetation, which can make them easier to hear than to see.
Their calls can sound rough and rasping, including repeated “cherrit-berrit”-type notes.
Yellow-bellied Bulbuls can keep repeating their calls every few seconds for quite a while.
They usually forage in the lower and middle levels of the forest rather than spending all their time high in the canopy.
Yellow-bellied Bulbuls eat both fruit and animal prey such as insects, making them omnivores.
Adults have been observed eating berries while giving animal prey to their young.
They lay eggs rather than giving birth to live young, as all bulbuls do.
Four recognised subspecies of Yellow-bellied Bulbul occur across the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and different parts of Borneo.
Different Yellow-bellied Bulbul subspecies are associated with different parts of Borneo, including western, central and north-eastern Borneo.
White-breasted Waterhens often walk with their short tails held up and repeatedly flick them while moving.
The rusty-red patch under the tail can be flashed as a visual signal to mates and chicks, or to show predators that they have been spotted.
They are most active around dawn and dusk rather than in the middle of the day.
White-breasted Waterhens make loud croaks, grunts and chuckling calls, especially around dawn and dusk.
They can search for food by probing their bills into mud or shallow water, and they can also pick food up by sight.
White-breasted Waterhens have been observed carefully washing small fish in water before eating them.
Their courtship can include bowing, touching bills and gentle nibbling between the pair.
A pair usually lays about 6–7 eggs, and the eggs hatch after around 19 days.
Both the male and female help incubate the eggs and care for the chicks.
Young White-breasted Waterhens can dive underwater when they sense danger, helping them escape predators.
The Asian Small-clawed Otter is the smallest otter species in the world.
Its claws do not extend beyond the pads of its fingers and toes, which gives it excellent dexterity.
Asian Small-clawed Otters often use their sensitive front paws, rather than their mouths, to feel for and catch food.
They can use at least 12 different vocalisations, including calls for greeting, contact, threats and alarms.
They also communicate through scent marks, which can carry information about identity, sex and reproductive condition.
Asian Small-clawed Otters can live in large family groups of up to about 15–20 individuals.
Even though they live in family groups, they usually hunt by themselves.
Older siblings can help their parents feed and care for younger pups.
Females can give birth to one to six pups after a pregnancy of about 68–72 days.
Young otters begin entering shallow water at around three months old, under their mother’s guidance.
The Bornean Partridge is found only on Borneo, making it an island-endemic bird.
It is about 27 cm long and weighs around 270 g.
It has patches of bare red skin around its throat, although these are usually partly hidden by feathers.
Females usually have slightly duller plumage than males.
Bornean Partridges often search for food in groups rather than always feeding alone.
They forage through dense thickets and may also search for food along forest roads and near rivers.
They roost in bushes when they rest.
Their song is often a duet between two birds.
During the duet, one bird gives rising notes while the other answers with falling notes.
They are often easier to hear than to see because they forage in dense forest undergrowth.
The Binturong is also called the “bearcat,” even though it is neither a bear nor a cat.
Binturongs can live about 16–18 years in the wild and may reach around 25 years in human care.
Its prehensile tail is almost as long as its body and can grip branches like a fifth limb.
The Binturong is one of only two carnivorous mammals with a prehensile tail.
Binturongs smell like buttered popcorn because their scent contains the same aroma compound found in popcorn.
They use their popcorn-like scent to mark their presence, communicate with other binturongs and help attract mates.
Binturongs can rotate their hind feet about 180° so they can climb down tree trunks head-first while keeping a strong grip.
They usually do not leap from tree to tree, so they may need to climb down to the ground before moving to another tree.
Female Binturongs can delay implantation, meaning a fertilised egg can wait before attaching to the uterus until conditions are more favourable.
Baby Binturongs are called “binlets,” and they are born with their eyes closed.
The Small-toothed Palm Civet is also called the Three-striped Palm Civet because it usually has three dark stripes or rows of spots running along its back.
It is almost completely arboreal, meaning it spends most of its life in trees and is rarely seen on the ground.
Its tail can be longer than its head and body combined, and it is somewhat prehensile, helping the civet grip while climbing.
Fleshy pads underneath its feet give it a strong grip on branches while climbing through trees.
Small-toothed Palm Civets are mainly active at night and may spend the daytime resting on branches high in the canopy.
They are usually solitary, but several individuals have sometimes been seen feeding together in the same fruiting fig tree.
Their unusual small, widely spaced teeth are poorly suited for slicing meat, which is one reason fruit is thought to be especially important in their diet.
Females can breed throughout the year and may produce two litters in a year, usually with two or three young each time.
Pregnancy lasts only about 45 days, and the young are weaned at around 61 days old.
Small-toothed Palm Civets can live around 10–12 years in the wild, and reticulated pythons are among their recorded predators.
Male Great Argus birds are among the largest pheasants and can reach around 1.6–2 metres in total length, mostly because of their extremely long tail feathers.
Young males do not develop their full adult plumage until about their third year.
A male clears an open patch on the forest floor to create his own dancing ground before displaying to females.
Before dancing, the male gives loud calls to advertise his presence and attract females.
During courtship, he spreads his enormous wing feathers into two huge fans covered with hundreds of eye-like markings.
During the display, the male bows his head so low that it can become hidden behind the fan of feathers.
Female Great Argus birds are much smaller than males and have shorter tails and fewer eye-spots.
Great Argus birds usually search for food on the forest floor in the early morning and evening.
A female usually lays only two eggs, which is a very small clutch compared with many other ground birds.
Although their spectacular display once led people to think they were polygamous, published accounts cited for the species describe Great Argus as monogamous.
Asiatic Brush-tailed Porcupines are nocturnal and usually search for food at night.
On full-moon nights, they may limit their activity to dawn and dusk, which researchers linked to avoiding predators.
The end of the tail has a brush-like cluster of unusual flattened quills that look a little like strings of beads.
They are surprisingly agile and can run, climb and swim well.
They may travel as far as about 15 kilometres in a single night while searching for food.
Family groups can contain around four to eight porcupines that share trails, feeding places, shelters and territory.
Although they shelter together during the day, they usually go out to forage alone at night.
Their rock dens can be surprisingly complex, with several entrances connected to tunnels about 3.5 metres long.
Females usually have one or two young per litter, and both parents help guard and care for them.
Newborns are unusually well developed: they can be active and agile within hours of birth and open their eyes very soon after being born.
The gaur is the largest living species of wild cattle.
Both male and female gaurs have horns that curve upward from the sides of the head.
Gaur herds are usually led by an older adult female called the matriarch.
At some times of year, gaur live in small herds of about 8–11 animals, but several herds can sometimes join into groups of 50 or more.
Adult males may leave female herds and live alone or form all-male bachelor groups.
During the breeding season, a male gaur’s loud bellow can be heard from more than 1.6 kilometres away.
Gaurs also use a high whistling snort as an alarm call when they sense danger.
Despite their enormous size, gaurs can move through the forest surprisingly quickly when alarmed.
Female gaurs usually give birth to one calf after a pregnancy of about 275 days.
Gaur calves may stay with their mothers for 7–12 months before they are fully weaned.
Banteng are wild cattle that are also known as tembadau.
Banteng live socially in herds that can contain up to about 40 animals.
A typical family group has one adult male together with several females.
Both male and female banteng calves are born with reddish coats.
During their first year, young banteng develop their white “stockings” and pale rump patches.
As male banteng grow up, their coats gradually darken from reddish brown to black, while adult females remain chestnut-coloured.
Banteng are generally described as shy, tolerant and less territorial than many other wild cattle.
Banteng can be active both during the day and at night, and may become more nocturnal in places with more human activity.
The banteng became the first endangered species to be successfully cloned, in 2004.
Banteng have also reproduced successfully through artificial insemination and embryo transfer, techniques that may help conservation breeding.
Barred Eagle-Owls have two long ear tufts that stick out sideways, giving them a distinctive horned appearance.
Adults have extremely dark, almost black-looking eyes, while young birds are much paler and can appear almost milky white.
Their territorial call is a deep resonant hoot, and they can also make screams, howls and noisy cackling sounds.
When they give a double territorial hoot, the two hoots can be separated by about two seconds.
Barred Eagle-Owls are thought to form long-lasting pairs and may stay in the same territory for several years.
They can nest inside large tree cavities, but some have also nested on top of large bird’s-nest ferns.
A female normally lays only one egg at a time.
Barred Eagle-Owls have powerful feet and large curved talons that allow them to catch surprisingly large prey.
Their prey can include insects, birds, rodents, snakes and other small animals.
Young Barred Eagle-Owls look very different from adults: juveniles are much paler, often appearing milky white with faint grey barring.
Green-backed Herons are clever hunters that can use bait, such as insects, feathers or leaves, to attract fish to the water’s surface.
They can stay very still at the water’s edge and wait patiently before striking at prey.
Because their legs are fairly short for a heron, they often crouch on rocks or at the water’s edge instead of wading deeply.
Their warning call is a loud, harsh double croak, so they may be heard before they are seen.
Green-backed Herons are usually solitary and are commonly seen hunting by themselves.
They can be territorial and may patrol their own stretch of shoreline or mangrove.
Their nests are shallow platforms made from sticks and are usually hidden among trees or bushes.
A female typically lays about 2–5 pale blue or green eggs.
Young Green-backed Herons look different from adults: juveniles are browner and have much more streaking on their bodies.
When threatened, young birds may stretch their necks upward and point their bills toward the sky.

The tip of its tail is black in all known populations.
Its belly is usually grey, although reddish colouring can sometimes appear along its sides.
Its upper fur can appear grey, yellowish-olive or reddish depending on the season and population.
In northern populations, its coat can turn bright orange or reddish during the dry season and become grey again during the wet season.
It often comes down from the trees and spends time on the ground.
It is generally not very shy and may come close to places where people live.
It eats a varied diet that includes fruits, seeds and tree bark, as well as some insects.
It can live in many different environments, including primary forests, secondary forests, bamboo areas, parks and gardens.
The Grey-bellied Squirrel has been introduced to the Ryukyu Islands of Japan, outside its native range.
The Plantain Squirrel has two cream-and-black stripes along its sides, an orange belly, and no pale spot behind its ears.
It is very quick and agile in trees and can jump a few metres from one tree to another, while rarely spending much time on the ground.
It communicates with shrill chattering and a chirping sound like “tswit,” often waving or flourishing its tail while calling.
Plantain Squirrels use different alarm responses for different predators: they may approach and mob a snake, but freeze and quickly take cover when a bird of prey appears.
It can break open twigs to reach and eat ant larvae hidden inside.
It can eat fruits much larger than itself, including mangoes, jackfruit and coconuts.
It sometimes gnaws the bark of trees, including rubber trees, to obtain sap or latex.
Its nest is shaped like a ball and is made from twigs and leaves, lined with fur, with a round entrance hole. These nests can be built around 5 metres or more above the ground.
After about 40 days of pregnancy, a female usually gives birth to 1–4 babies, which are born blind and without hair.
Young Plantain Squirrels usually leave their nest when they are about six weeks old.

Its fur has a grizzled appearance because individual hairs are banded with dark and pale brown colours.
When threatened, it can spray a strong-smelling fluid from glands near the base of its tail as a defence.
It has well-developed senses of smell and hearing, which help it detect what is happening around it.
It is an excellent swimmer and often searches for prey along streams and close to water.
Despite its name, it does not eat only crabs—it also catches fish, snails, frogs, rodents, birds, reptiles and insects.
Crab-eating Mongooses are often active during the morning and evening and have been observed travelling in groups of up to four.
One was observed digging into the nest of an Impressed Tortoise, probably searching for eggs to eat.
Compared with its body, it has a relatively short, bushy tail, along with a small head, hunched back and short, thin legs.
The soles of its hind feet are hairy, and its tail can have a paler tip.
The Long-tailed Sibia has an exceptionally long tail and looks small-headed and slender compared with many other sibias.
Its body is mostly grey, while its wings and tail are noticeably darker.
It has a small but noticeable white patch near the tip of its wing.
Long-tailed Sibias often search for food together in flocks rather than feeding alone.
They are often heard before they are seen because they make a loud, chittering rattle.
They can live in several types of woodland, including evergreen, oak and pine forests.
They also use disturbed areas such as secondary growth, forest edges and scrub where large trees remain.
The species has a very wide range, stretching from the Himalayas through Southeast Asia all the way to Sumatra.
Malaysia has its own recognised subspecies of Long-tailed Sibia called Heterophasia picaoides wrayi.
Long-tailed Sibias are especially associated with open hill forests, where they move through forest edges and nearby scrub in groups.
The Blue-headed Pitta is about 17 cm long.
The male has a striking electric-blue crown, white throat, chestnut-brown back and dark blue or violet-blue underparts.
Females are much less colourful than males, with a warm cinnamon or buff-coloured head and brownish body.
Both males and females have dark wings marked with a noticeable white streak.
Its song is a mellow call that sounds roughly like “puh-yih-wooooo.”
The Blue-headed Pitta is found only on the island of Borneo, including Sabah and Sarawak in Malaysia, Brunei and Kalimantan in Indonesia.
It is most common in primary tropical lowland forest, although it can also live in logged or secondary forest.
It usually lives below about 600 metres above sea level.
Its nest is a round dome made from leaves, with an entrance on the side, and is built on or very close to the ground.
Blue-headed Pittas appear to breed seasonally: breeding birds have been recorded from March to June, while young birds have been found in nests between May and October.
The male is extremely colourful, with a black head, yellow-orange stripe above the eye, orange-red nape, yellow throat, blue belly and blue tail.
Its chest has bands of orange and dark blue, with more orange towards the sides and more blue towards the centre.
Malayan Banded Pittas spend much of their time on the ground in dense forest, quietly searching the forest floor for food.
Their most common calls include a quiet, low sound and a short descending “pr-r-r-r-r” call.
They mainly eat insects and fruits.
They are found naturally in Malaysia, southern Thailand and Sumatra.
They usually live in primary lowland evergreen forests and can also occur in swamp forests.
Although mainly a lowland forest bird, the Malayan Banded Pitta has been recorded at elevations of up to about 1,500 metres.
It can also live in secondary forest, but may not survive as well there as it does in primary forest.
The Malayan, Bornean and Javan banded pittas were once treated as one species, but they were separated after scientists found differences in their appearance, behaviour and calls.
The Bornean Banded Pitta is found only on the island of Borneo, including parts of Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.
It has a broad, bright yellow stripe above its eyes and a bold black mask across its face.
Its back is coffee-brown, while its underparts are covered with many fine dark bands.
Male Bornean Banded Pittas have a black crown, yellow throat and a striking indigo-blue patch on the belly.
Females are duller than males: they have a pale brown crown, whitish throat and no indigo-blue belly patch.
Its song is a series of powerful but mellow calls that sound roughly like “byow!” with pauses between each note.
It lives in both lowland and hill dipterocarp forests.
Within forests, it appears to favour dry ridges, hilltops and areas with limestone.
The Bornean Banded Pitta is a resident bird, meaning it does not normally migrate seasonally away from Borneo.
It was once considered the same species as the Malayan and Javan Banded Pittas, but today all three are recognised as separate species.
Dusky Leaf Monkeys have thick white rings around their eyes, making them look as if they are wearing spectacles. They also have a pale, hairless area around the mouth.
Baby Dusky Leaf Monkeys are born with bright yellow or orange fur, which gradually changes to the darker colour of adults as they grow.
An adult's fur can appear greyish-brown, dark grey or almost black, while the fur on its crown, legs and tail is usually lighter.
Its tail can be 70–80 cm long, which can be longer than its 50–70 cm head-and-body length.
Dusky Leaf Monkeys can live in troops of up to about 20 individuals.
Adult males help watch for possible predators and patrol the group's home range.
They are especially active in the early morning and late afternoon, while around midday they may rest in the shade of trees.
They spend most of their time in trees, but adults sometimes come down to the ground at forest edges to feed on low-growing shrubs.
They communicate using several types of sounds, including snorts, hoots, murmurs and squeaks.
They have a four-chambered stomach that helps them break down the tough cellulose found in leaves, somewhat like the digestive system of a cow or antelope.
Its legs are extremely thin, described as being about as thin as pencils and its hind legs are longer than its front legs.
Male Greater Mouse-deer do not have horns or antlers. Instead, they have elongated upper canine teeth that look like small tusks.
They are mainly nocturnal, meaning they are most active at night.
They usually live alone and travel along small trails through thick forest vegetation.
Male Greater Mouse-deer are territorial and mark their territory using urine, droppings and scent from a gland underneath the chin.
When an adult male becomes angry, it can stamp its hooves on the ground about four times every second.
They eat many kinds of plants, including fallen fruit, aquatic plants, buds, leaves, shrubs and grasses.
They often live near water and can be found in tropical forests, wet swampy areas and mangrove thickets.
A female usually gives birth to just one young after a pregnancy lasting about 152–155 days.
Newborn Greater Mouse-deer can stand almost immediately after birth and can become fully active within about 30 minutes.
Its flattened quills usually lie flat against its body, making it look more like a large spiny rat than many other porcupines.
Its quills are less than 5 cm long, making them the shortest quills among Old World porcupines.
The brush-like hollow quills near the tip of its tail do not make a rattling sound when shaken, unlike those of some other porcupines.
Its long tail can break off if it is grabbed, which may help it escape a predator, but the lost tail does not grow back.
It is nocturnal, spending most of the day resting in underground shelters and becoming active at night.
Although it spends most of its time on the ground, it is a surprisingly good climber and can climb trees and shrubs while searching for food.
Its broad paws have four toes on the front feet and five toes on the back feet, helping it climb effectively.
When frightened, it can fluff out its quills to look larger and pound its feet on the ground.
When running along the forest floor, it holds its long tail straight up.
It mainly eats plant material such as fruits, seeds, bamboo shoots and the soft layer beneath tree bark, but it may also eat insects and other small invertebrates.
The Chestnut-necklaced Partridge is about 26–32 cm long.
It has a rusty or chestnut-coloured upper breast with a dark, speckled collar above it.
Its throat is mostly white with fine dark speckles, while a pale orange patch can be seen near its ear.
Its yellow legs help distinguish it from other similar partridges living in the same region.
The female is slightly smaller and usually a little duller in colour than the male.
It is a shy bird that usually searches for food on the forest floor in small groups.
Its food includes seeds, berries and termites.
Pairs often sing together in a duet, producing loud, trembling whistles.
It usually lives at lower elevations than other partridge species found in the same area.
It lives mainly in lowland evergreen forest but can also occur in secondary forest.
The White-crowned Hornbill has a large, bushy white crest that stands upright on top of its head.
Males and females look very different: males are white from the head down to the belly, while females are mostly black and have a white crest.
Its wings are mostly black, but pale or white edges become especially noticeable when the bird is flying.
Unlike many hornbills, it often searches for food in the lower levels of the forest and may even come down to the ground.
White-crowned Hornbills are social birds and often search for food together in groups.
Their calls include soft, owl-like hooting and cooing sounds.
They eat many different foods, including fruits, lizards, arthropods and insect larvae.
They occur naturally in the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo.
A nesting female seals herself inside a tree hole using materials such as mud, droppings and debris, leaving only a narrow opening.
While the female is sealed inside the nest, the male and other members of the group pass food to her and the chicks through the narrow opening.
The Sunda Laughingthrush is a medium-sized bird, measuring about 24–25 cm long.
It has a slate-grey head and chest, chestnut-brown wings and tail, and a distinctive pale blue ring around its eyes.
Male and female Sunda Laughingthrushes look very similar, while young birds are generally duller in colour than adults.
When searching for food on the forest floor, it can pick up and flip over fallen leaves to uncover food hiding underneath.
Its diet includes insects such as beetles, moths and caterpillars, as well as seeds and fruits.
Sunda Laughingthrushes are social birds and may travel in groups of up to about 12, sometimes joining other bird species while searching for food.
They are very vocal and can make noisy whistles as well as unusual calls that sound like a cat mewing.
There are two recognised subspecies: one occurs on Sumatra and the other occurs on Borneo.
The Bornean subspecies has been recorded from about 300–2,010 metres above sea level, while the Sumatran subspecies mainly occurs from about 850–2,200 metres.
Their breeding season differs between the islands: records indicate around March–April in Sumatra and December–March in Borneo.
The Orange-headed Thrush is a small thrush, measuring about 20.5–23.5 cm long.
Adult males have a bright orange head and underparts that contrast strongly with their plain grey upperparts and wings.
Females have browner or more olive-coloured upperparts than males, while young birds are dull brown with streaks on their backs.
It is a shy and secretive bird, and when disturbed it may stay completely still until the danger has passed.
It usually searches for food on the ground, probing through fallen leaves and dense undergrowth, especially around dawn and dusk.
Its diet includes insects, insect larvae, earthworms, spiders, fruit and other small invertebrates; birds in Malaysia also feed on figs.
Its song is a series of clear musical notes, and it can imitate other birds such as bulbuls, babblers and Common Tailorbirds.
Both the male and female help build the nest, making a shallow cup from twigs, roots and plant material and lining it with softer materials such as leaves and moss.
A nest usually contains three or four eggs; the eggs hatch after about 13–14 days, and the young can leave the nest about 12 days later.
Orange-headed Thrushes are usually seen alone or in pairs rather than in flocks, although several may gather where there is a particularly good food source.
The Chestnut-capped Thrush is a small thrush, measuring roughly 16–18 cm long.
Its chestnut-coloured crown continues down onto the back of its neck, giving the bird its “chestnut-capped” name.
Its face is mostly black but has contrasting white patches on the cheeks and between the eyes and bill.
Its dark grey or blackish back contrasts with two noticeable broad white markings on its wings.
Its throat and upper breast are very dark, while its lower breast is covered with black spots that fade into a white belly.
It spends much of its feeding time on the forest floor, searching through leaf litter for invertebrates such as earthworms.
It mainly lives in lowland forest with dense vegetation, but it can also occur in secondary and previously logged forest.
The Chestnut-capped Thrush is a secretive bird that usually stays low in the forest, making it difficult to spot even when it is nearby.
Its range extends across parts of Southeast Asia, including the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Borneo and several nearby islands.
The Enggano Thrush was once treated as a subspecies of the Chestnut-capped Thrush, but it is now recognised separately, leaving the Chestnut-capped Thrush with no recognised subspecies.
The Malayan Night Heron is a medium-sized heron, measuring about 48–51 cm long.
Adults have a dark cinnamon-brown body, a black crown and a dark stripe running from the throat down towards the breast.
Young Malayan Night Herons look very different from adults, with grey-brown plumage covered in pale bars and markings.
During the breeding season, adults can develop a bright blue patch of bare skin between the bill and the eyes; this colour becomes duller outside the breeding season.
They are usually solitary birds rather than gathering in large groups.
They are mainly active around dusk and at night, although they can sometimes be seen feeding during the daytime.
When hunting, they may stand completely still or walk very slowly before catching prey.
Earthworms and frogs are important foods, but they can also eat insects, fish, snails, crabs, spiders and reptiles.
They can live in forests and forest edges as well as wooded parks and gardens, and they may also occur near streams and marshes.
Their territorial call consists of deep “oo” notes, and they can also make rough croaking calls.
The Common Hill Myna measures about 27–31 cm long.
It has glossy black feathers with a purple-green shine, bright yellow wattles on its head, an orange bill and yellow legs.
It has white patches on its wings that become especially easy to see when the bird is flying.
Young Common Hill Mynas are duller and less glossy than adults, with a browner shade on their upperparts.
It mainly lives in mature humid forests and forest edges, but it can also occur in wooded parkland.
Common Hill Mynas are often seen in pairs or small groups, especially when gathering at fruiting trees.
It has an unusually wide range of natural calls, including screams, squeaks, chirps and whistles.
It is an omnivore that eats fruits, nectar and insects.
Common Hill Mynas build their nests inside holes in trees, and a nest usually contains two or three eggs.
The Common Hill Myna is famous for its ability to imitate sounds, including human speech.
A typical Prevost’s Squirrel has black upperparts and tail, reddish-orange underparts, and a white stripe along each side of its body.
Its body is about 20–27 cm long, and its bushy tail is roughly the same length as its body.
It is active during the day and spends almost all of its time in trees, only occasionally coming down to the ground.
Prevost’s Squirrels sometimes leave the forest to visit gardens and plantations when searching for ripe fruit.
Besides fruit, they can dig insects such as termites, ants and beetles out of rotting wood.
At night, they sleep in tree hollows or nests made from leaves and twigs, and they can wrap their bushy tails around themselves for warmth.
Newborn Prevost’s Squirrels are born naked, toothless, helpless and with their eyes closed, but by about six weeks they are fully furred and able to explore outside the nest.
They have been seen feeding together in groups at fig trees, even though squirrels are often thought of as solitary animals.
They help spread seeds by carrying fruit away from the parent tree and dropping the seeds after eating the flesh.

Prevost’s Squirrels use different alarm calls for different dangers, including separate warnings for flying predators, ground predators and snakes. They can also use their tails like flags to communicate.
A Serow can stand up to about 94 cm tall at the shoulder and weigh as much as 140 kg.
Its coat is usually dark grey to black, while young Serows may have greyer fur.
Older Serows develop a mane of long hair along their backs, which can appear greyish, buff or reddish.
Serows have short, pointed horns that curve slightly backwards and relatively large ears.
They are skilled at moving across steep, rocky and forested slopes despite their stocky bodies.
They can live high in the mountains and have been recorded at elevations of up to about 3,000 metres.
Serows usually live alone, although small groups have sometimes been observed.
They are mainly active during the day, although activity can also occur at other times.
Serows browse on many kinds of vegetation rather than relying on just one type of plant.
A female usually gives birth to a single young after a pregnancy lasting about eight months.
The Bornean Ground-Cuckoo is a large bird, measuring about 60 cm long.
It is found only on the island of Borneo, including parts of Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.
Unlike many cuckoos that spend much of their time in trees, this species spends most of its time walking and searching for food on the forest floor.
It has iridescent purple-green wings, a long dark tail, a black head and pale blue-green skin around its face and bill.
Its belly and other lower parts have striking fine black-and-white bars.
It is extremely secretive and is often heard calling before it is actually seen.
It lives mainly in humid forest and is especially associated with lowland forest near rivers and swampy areas.
It searches through leaf litter for food and mainly eats invertebrates such as insects.
It has sometimes been seen following Bearded Pigs or Sun Bears and eating small animals disturbed by these larger mammals as they move through the forest.
Male Bornean Ground-Cuckoos can make different calls, including a single “koo” and a two-note “thook-torr”; one observation found that the bird flicked its tail upward when giving the single call.
The Borneo Bay Cat is about the size of a large domestic cat, with a head-and-body length of about 53 cm and a tail around 39 cm long.
Its tail is unusually long compared with its body and tapers towards the end.
Bay Cats occur in different colour forms: some have rich chestnut-red fur, while others are grey, and very dark individuals have also been recorded.
Its face has dark stripes beginning near the corners of the eyes, and the back of its head can have a dark M-shaped marking.
The underside of its long tail has a pale stripe that becomes pure white near the tip, while the upper surface of the tail is dark.
The Borneo Bay Cat is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
The Borneo Bay Cat is mainly terrestrial, meaning it spends much of its time moving and hunting on the ground rather than in trees.
Bay Cats are mainly active during the daytime, with activity peaks in the morning and early afternoon.
Most Bay Cat sightings have been below 800 metres above sea level, but the species has been recorded as high as about 1,460 metres in the Kelabit Highlands.
The Bay Cat was once thought to be a small island form of the Asian Golden Cat, but genetic testing showed that it is its own distinct species.
The Asiatic Golden Cat is much larger than a domestic cat, with a head-and-body length of about 66–105 cm and a tail about 40–57 cm long.
Its coat can come in many colours, including golden, reddish-brown, grey and almost black; some individuals even have spotted “ocelot-like” patterns.
It has distinctive pale and dark stripes on the sides of its face.
The underside of its tail is white near the end, while the upper tip may be dark.
It spends most of its time on the ground, but it is also able to climb trees when needed.
Unlike animals that are active only by day or only by night, Asiatic Golden Cats have been recorded being active during both daytime and nighttime.
It hunts many kinds of animals, including birds, rats, squirrels, reptiles and small deer.
Females can shelter their young in hidden places such as hollow trees, spaces between rocks or hollows in the ground.
It can live in many different forest types, including primary forest, secondary forest and even dry forest near grasslands.
Although it is more commonly recorded in lowlands, it has also been found at elevations approaching 4,000 metres in Bhutan.
The Common Emerald Dove is about 23–27 cm long.
It gets its name from its bright emerald-green wings, which contrast with its reddish body and bright orange-red bill.
Male and female Common Emerald Doves look different: males have a large silver-grey or white crown and a white shoulder patch, while females lack the white shoulder patch and are generally browner.
Young Common Emerald Doves are duller and browner than adults, with rusty-coloured edges on some of their wing feathers.
They usually search for food alone or in pairs on the forest floor, eating seeds, fruits and insects.
Their call is a series of low, soft coos that starts quietly and becomes louder.
When disturbed, a Common Emerald Dove may walk away instead of immediately flying off.
During courtship, a male performs a bobbing dance to display to a female.
They can live in several wooded habitats, including secondary forest, forest edges, mangroves and coastal woodland.
They build a simple stick nest in a tree, sometimes up to about 5 metres above the ground, and usually lay two cream-coloured eggs.
The White-rumped Shama is about 21.5–28 cm long.
Adult males have a glossy blue-black head and back, an orange-rufous belly, a bright white rump and a long dark tail.
Females are more greyish-brown than males and usually have a shorter tail.
Young White-rumped Shamas are brownish like females but have buff speckles and dark, scale-like markings on the chest.
They usually search for food on the ground by moving through fallen leaves and other leaf litter.
They are shy and territorial birds, and a male will defend an area from other White-rumped Shamas.
During courtship, the male flicks and spreads his tail feathers and may perform a rising-and-falling flight with the female.
The female builds the nest by herself while the male stands guard nearby.
Their nests are often placed in tree hollows, and a female commonly lays four or five eggs.
The White-rumped Shama has a loud, clear and melodious song and can imitate the calls of other bird species.
The Rufous-tailed Shama is about 20–22 cm long.
Adult males have a dark grey to almost black head, breast and wings, which contrast with their bright orange-rufous belly and rump.
A male has a small bright white patch just above or in front of the eye, while the female does not have this white marking.
Females are browner than males, with an olive-brown head and upperparts and a buff or rufous-coloured breast.
Most of its tail is bright rufous or orange, but the feathers become dark grey or black towards the tip.
It occurs naturally in extreme southern Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo.
It lives mainly in moist lowland forests and can also occur in tropical swamp forests.
The Rufous-tailed Shama is mainly a terrestrial bird, spending much of its time at or near ground level.
It is a resident bird rather than a seasonal migrant, meaning it generally stays within its range throughout the year.
It was once placed in its own genus, Trichixos, but genetic research led scientists to move it into the genus Copsychus.
The Oriental Magpie-robin is about 19–21 cm long.
Adult males have glossy black upperparts and breast, a white belly, a bold white wing stripe and white outer tail feathers.
Females resemble males but have dark grey instead of glossy black on the head, breast and upperparts.
Young birds are browner than adults and have scale-like markings on their upper breast and body.
When searching for food on the ground, they often hop around with their long tail held upright.
They mainly eat insects and other small invertebrates, but have also been recorded eating foods such as nectar, geckos, leeches, centipedes and even fish.
Males sing loudly from high perches, and their songs can even imitate the calls of other bird species.
During courtship, a male may puff up his feathers, raise his bill, fan his tail and strut to attract a female.
They often build nests inside tree holes, wall cavities or nest boxes, lining the space with grass.
The female usually lays four or five pale blue-green eggs with brownish speckles and incubates them by herself for about 8–14 days.
The Blue-breasted Quail is the smallest and lightest bird in the order Galliformes, the group that includes chickens, pheasants and other quails.
Adult males have a blue head and breast, a deep cinnamon-coloured belly, and bold black-and-white markings on the throat.
Females are mostly brown with a paler belly and a plain face, making them much less colourful than males.
Its call includes a descending whistle that sounds like “tew-tew,” as well as a rough, snoring call.
It spends most of its life on the ground and usually stays hidden among grasses and other low vegetation.
When suddenly disturbed, it can burst rapidly upward into flight to escape danger.
It can live in lowland grasslands, grassy hillsides and farmland.
Its wild diet includes grass seeds, other small seeds, vegetation and tiny insects.
A female can lay a clutch of about 5–13 eggs before she begins incubating them.
The chicks hatch after roughly 16 days of incubation.
The Malaysian Rail-babbler is about 28–30 cm long and has a long neck, long legs and a long tail.
It has a reddish-brown crown and a rich chestnut throat, with a broad white stripe above the eye and a bold black stripe running through the eye.
It has a strip of bare blue skin on the side of its neck that becomes easier to see when the bird calls or displays.
Males and females look alike, while young birds are duller and have a whitish throat and darker grey-brown belly.
It spends most of its time on the forest floor and walks in a rail-like way, jerking its head somewhat like a chicken.
When frightened, it usually prefers to run away and hide rather than immediately fly.
It hunts insects such as cicadas and beetles, as well as spiders and worms, and may dash after prey on the forest floor.
Its usual call is a long, repeated whistle, but when agitated it can produce a series of unusual frog-like notes.
Its cup-shaped nest is made from plant fibres and can be placed very close to the ground among dead leaves and plant stems.
The Malaysian Rail-babbler can live from lowland forest up into lower mountain forest, reaching about 1,060 metres above sea level in Peninsular Malaysia.
The Malaysian Mole is found naturally only in Peninsular Malaysia, making it the southernmost known mole species in the world.
It is known only from the Cameron Highlands.
It has been recorded at elevations of about 1,300–1,600 metres above sea level.
Malaysian Moles have been found in tea plantations and nearby gardens.
The species was first discovered in 1937 in a forest that was being converted into a tea plantation.
Scientists once suspected that the Malaysian Mole had accidentally arrived with tea plants brought from Darjeeling, India, but later genetic evidence showed that it is native to Malaysia.
Genetic and physical studies found that it is most closely related to Kloss’s Mole rather than the Himalayan Mole.
Compared with the length of its skull, its upper molars are proportionally larger than those of any other mole in the genus Euroscaptor.
Scientists think it may be a relict species that survived in the Cameron Highlands because the cooler mountain climate is suitable for moles.
Malaysia’s hot tropical lowlands are thought to be unsuitable for this mole because they have poorer soil development and less leaf litter than the cooler highlands.
A Common Sun Skink can reach about 35 cm from its snout to the end of its tail, while its body alone is about 13 cm long.
Its body is usually bronze-brown and may have thin black stripes running along its back.
Some Common Sun Skinks have dark sides covered with white spots, while others have a bright orange band stretching from behind the ear towards the hind legs.
Each scale on its back usually has three raised ridges, called keels.
It is active during the daytime and is often seen basking in sunny places on rocks, logs, tree trunks or the ground.
When approached, it usually tries to escape quickly by running away.
When under stress or threatened, a Common Sun Skink can shed its tail as a defence.
Its food consists mainly of insects.
Unlike reptiles that lay eggs, the Common Sun Skink gives birth to live young.
It can be identified by five or seven dark lines running lengthwise along the underside of its body.
The Yellow-rumped Flycatcher is a small bird, measuring about 13–13.5 cm long.
Adult males have black upperparts, bright yellow underparts and rump, a broad white eyebrow, and a long white patch on the wings.
Females are much duller than males, with greyish-olive upperparts and pale underparts, but they still have the species’ distinctive yellow rump.
During spring, males can develop an orange flush on their throat and breast.
The yellow rump is visible in males, females and young birds, making it one of the most useful features for identifying the species.
It is a migratory bird: it breeds in eastern Asia and travels south to spend the winter mainly in the Thai-Malay Peninsula and Sumatra.
During migration and winter, it can use many different habitats, including forests, parks, gardens, wooded areas and mangroves.
The female builds the nest by herself, usually completing it in about three to four days.
A female usually lays several eggs and incubates them by herself for around 11–12 days.
Young Yellow-rumped Flycatchers usually leave the nest about 14–15 days after hatching.
Male Red Junglefowl are much larger than females: males measure about 65–78 cm long, while females are about 41–46 cm.
Adult males have a bright red comb, white ear patches, golden-yellow neck feathers and a curved dark-green tail.
Females are much less colourful than males, with mostly golden-brown plumage that helps them blend into their surroundings.
Male Red Junglefowl change appearance during their yearly “eclipse” moult: their long colourful neck feathers are replaced by shorter, duller feathers for several months.
They spend most of their time on the ground, but they can fly into trees and other high places to roost safely at night.
Red Junglefowl regularly take dust baths, which help remove excess oil from their feathers.
They use different alarm calls for dangers in the air and dangers on the ground, and other birds respond differently depending on the warning.
Adults eat more plant material such as fruits and seeds, while chicks depend much more heavily on insects, insect larvae and earthworms.
Male Red Junglefowl perform a courtship behaviour called “tidbitting”: they make clucking sounds, bob their heads and repeatedly pick up and drop food to attract a female.
The Red Junglefowl is the main wild ancestor of today’s domestic chicken.
The thick-spined porcupine is quite adaptable. It can live in wild forests and also in places where people grow crops.
This porcupine can live from low ground near sea level all the way up to at least 1,200 metres, higher than many city skyscrapers!
The thick-spined porcupine is a true Borneo special. In the wild, it is naturally found only on this island, including the Malaysian part of Borneo.
The thick-spined porcupine keeps its paws on solid ground. It is a land-living animal rather than one that lives in water or trees.
Thick-spined porcupines can live in natural forests and even in areas where people grow crops.
Wildlife status can change as scientists learn more. The thick-spined porcupine was listed as Near Threatened in 1996, but by 2008 it had moved to Least Concern.
Surprise, a porcupine is a rodent! The thick-spined porcupine belongs to the same huge mammal group as animals such as rats and squirrels.
People hunt this porcupine for food, but scientists cited by these sources say its broad range and ability to handle changed habitats help the species cope with this pressure.
The thick-spined porcupine is not limited to deep jungle. It can also live around agricultural land changed by people.
The thick-spined porcupine has another cool name, the Borneo short-tailed porcupine, which hints at both its island home and its short tail
No giant seasonal journey for this bird. The striped wren-babbler stays around its home range all year instead of migrating with the seasons.
There are signs that the striped wren-babbler's population is shrinking, which makes protecting its habitat especially important.
The striped wren-babbler likes warm, wet places. You can find its natural habitat in damp lowland forests and swampy areas.
The striped wren-babbler has a whole genus to itself. It is the one and only species placed in Kenopia.
Like other egg-laying birds, the striped wren-babbler starts life by hatching from an egg.
You can find the striped wren-babbler in Malaysia, but Malaysia does not have it all to itself. The bird also lives in Brunei, Indonesia, and Thailand.
This bird's scientific naming has a two-part history. Its species name dates to 1842, but its genus, Kenopia, was established 27 years later in 1869.
The striped wren-babbler is a land-loving forest bird. The bird is terrestrial and is an important part of the forest biome.
The striped wren-babbler belongs to a huge bird group called Passeriformes, also known as the passerines.
This bird does not mind soggy surroundings. The striped wren-babbler can live around swampy places as well as wet lowland forests.
This owl may look big, but it is actually the smallest fish owl species. A buffy fish owl can grow about 40 to 48 cm long and weigh roughly 1 to 2.1 kg.
This owl goes fishing without taking a swim. The buffy fish owl can swoop from the riverbank or step into shallow water and grab prey with its feet while keeping its feathers dry.
Not every owl is a silent flyer. The buffy fish owl lacks some of the special fluffy feather edges that quiet other owls, so its wings can actually make noise in flight.

Fish may be in the name, but this owl is not a fish-only eater. The buffy fish owl can munch on crabs, frogs, reptiles and birds, and researchers have even found evidence of insects, rats, and fruit bats in its diet.
This owl has a whole sound collection. Buffy fish owls can hiss, rattle out calls, and make loud or high notes. A pair may even perform an owl duet together for several minutes.
Talk about unusual bedrooms. A buffy fish owl may nest on top of a giant fern, inside a tree hole, or sometimes even behind a waterfall.

One egg is a big deal for this owl. Buffy fish owl nests have only been recorded with one egg per breeding season. The egg takes about 28 to 29 days to hatch, and the youngster is ready to fledge around six weeks later.

Protecting wildlife matters close to home. In Johor in 2008, authorities found 14 buffy fish owls in an illegal wildlife shipment, showing that these Malaysian owls can be targeted by wildlife trafficking.
The buffy fish owl is right at home in Malaysia. Look for its kind of habitat near forests, rivers, lakes, and wetlands, from lowlands all the way up to about 1,600 m high.
Most owls cough up neat little pellets, but the buffy fish owl does things differently. Bits of bones and other leftovers can come out separately and drop below its resting spot.
Malaysia is part of this bird's winter holiday zone. Some tiger shrikes keep flying even farther, reaching islands such as Java, Bali, and Sulawesi.

You do not always need to hike high into the mountains to find tiger shrike habitat. In winter, the tiger shrike usually stays below 1,000 metres and can turn up near forests, farms, mangroves, and gardens.
Why is it called a tiger shrike? Check out its back. Dark stripes cross reddish-brown feathers, giving the bird its own tiny tiger pattern.
A tiger shrike can change its look depending on its age and sex. Adult males wear a bold black "mask", while females are browner and youngsters do not yet have the same grey and black head markings.
The tiger shrike may be a fierce little hunter, but it is only about 17 to 19 cm long. Females have been recorded at up to 37 g, while males in the cited measurements weighed 27 to 29 g.
Do not let its small size fool you. The tiger shrike loves insects like grasshoppers and beetles, but it can also hunt lizards, tiny birds, and even rodents.
This hunter can use two strategies. A tiger shrike may wait quietly on a perch for prey to appear, or sneak through leafy branches searching for its next meal.
Tiger shrike romance comes with a dance show. A male can bob his body, wiggle his head from side to side, sing softly, then zoom through a fast display flight.

Building a tiger shrike family is teamwork. Mum and dad both help make the nest, usually above the ground in a tree. There are often five eggs, Mum sits on them for about 14 to 16 days, and the chicks leave the nest roughly two weeks after hatching
Tiger shrikes may travel across a huge part of Asia, but scientists currently do not split them into different subspecies. They are all treated as the same tiger shrike species.
"Earless" does not mean deaf. The Borneo earless monitor can hear, but you cannot see normal ear openings on the sides of its head.
This lizard likes life close to water. The Borneo earless monitor usually lives below 300 m near streams and marshes, and it can even survive near farms and oil palm areas if suitable streams remain.
This lizard is a night explorer. By day, the Borneo earless monitor may hide in a burrow about 30 cm long or tuck itself under logs, rocks, and plants.
Underwater snack time! The Borneo earless monitor eats worms, crustaceans, and fish, and it can do something unusual for a lizard, swallow its food while still underwater.
A typical adult Borneo earless monitor is around 40 cm from nose to tail, about the length of a large school ruler plus a little extra.
Its tail can work a bit like an extra grip. The Borneo earless monitor can use its prehensile tail to hold on, but if the tail is lost, it will not grow back.
A Borneo earless monitor mum can lay anywhere from 2 to 12 eggs, with about 8 being typical. At 27°C in captivity, the eggs take around three months to hatch.
Malaysia gives this rare lizard serious protection. In Sarawak, the Borneo earless monitor is a Totally Protected Animal and is listed locally as "Cicak purba."
This secretive lizard needs protection. The Borneo earless monitor is Endangered, its known range is very small, and wildlife trafficking and habitat loss can put extra pressure on the species.
This lizard has an entire family all to itself. The Borneo earless monitor is the only living member of Lanthanotidae, making it a very unusual survivor on the lizard family tree.
The crab-eating macaque is a true Southeast Asian monkey, and Malaysia is one of the countries it naturally calls home.
Now that is a long tail! A crab-eating macaque's tail can be about as long as its whole head and body put together.
Jungle, mangrove, or even the edge of a town, the crab-eating macaque can adjust to many different neighbourhoods.
Despite the name "crab-eating," this monkey is a big fruit fan. In some wild groups, fruit makes up more than 80% of the menu.
These monkeys have their own stone tool kit. Some crab-eating macaques pick up rocks and use them like hammers to smash open tough snacks.
A crab-eating macaque can help plant the forest without even trying. By eating fruit and spreading seeds, it helps new plants grow in different places.
In a crab-eating macaque troop, daughters usually stay with their family, but sons eventually head off to another group. A troop can contain dozens of monkeys.
Baby crab-eating macaques arrive wearing a dark coat. Their fur starts changing from black to greyish or reddish brown when they are around three months old.
Monkey friendship can cross species. In Malaysia, researchers have seen crab-eating macaques grooming Raffles' banded langurs, almost like giving another kind of monkey a furry spa treatment.
Crab-eating macaques can learn table manners from each other. Some wash or rub their food before eating, and youngsters may copy what older monkeys do.
Its short tail is usually held partly upright, making it resemble a pig’s tail, which is how the Pig-tailed Macaque got its common name.
It has a stocky body with creamy-brown fur on its sides, darker fur along its back, pale underparts and a dark brown patch on the crown of its head.
It can be distinguished from the closely related Northern Pig-tailed Macaque because it does not have the diagonal facial lines that extend upward from the corners of the eyes.
Southern Pig-tailed Macaques are active during the day and spend about half of their daily activity on the ground, although they are also skilled tree climbers.
They can live in large groups, but the group often splits into smaller groups of about 2–6 individuals while searching for food and comes back together later.
They are omnivores, but most of their diet is plant-based and includes fruits, shoots, leaves, flowers, fungi and bark, along with insects and other small animals.
Their colour vision helps them distinguish red from green, which makes it easier to find ripe red or orange fruits among green leaves.
They communicate using many sounds, including coos, barks, grunts and screams, and can combine these sounds with facial expressions.
In the 19th century, “bruh” was a native name used by Malays in Sumatra for the Southern Pig-tailed Macaque.
A mother usually gives birth to one baby after a pregnancy of about six months, and newborns have black fur that gradually changes to their adult colouring as they grow.
The Sooty-capped Babbler is a small bird, measuring about 15.5–17 cm long.
It has a dark brown or blackish cap, olive-brown upperparts, a dull chestnut tail and whitish underparts.
Male and female Sooty-capped Babblers look very similar to each other.
It mainly eats small insects, including ants, beetles and caterpillars.
It often searches for food in pairs or small groups, picking insects from leaves and other vegetation.
Its song consists of clear whistles that can move up and down in pitch and may sound surprisingly human-like.
It can join mixed-species flocks, travelling and feeding alongside other kinds of forest birds.
It can live along forest edges and tracks and has also been recorded in peat-swamp forest, selectively logged forest and overgrown plantations.
It is a resident bird, meaning it normally stays within the same region throughout the year instead of making long seasonal migrations.
Its nest is a shallow cup made from materials such as dead leaves, twigs and plant fibres, and a recorded clutch contains two eggs.
The Yellow-throated Marten has a striking multicoloured coat, combining yellow or golden fur with dark brown or black areas on its body and tail.
Its body is about 45–65 cm long, while its thick tail can add another 37–45 cm.
It has a small head with a pointed muzzle, rounded ears, an elongated body and powerful hind legs.
It moves with a fast, bounding gait that can look similar to the movement of a large squirrel.
It is mainly active during the daytime.
Yellow-throated Martens are comfortable both on the ground and in trees, making them both terrestrial and arboreal.
Their varied diet includes squirrels, reptiles, insects, fruits and berries, and they are even reported to enjoy honey.
They have been seen eating bees directly at the entrances of bee nests.
They are usually seen alone, although small family groups can sometimes travel together.
They can live in both lowland and mountain forests and have been recorded at elevations of up to about 3,000 metres.
The Bornean Yellow Muntjac is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
Its fur is usually yellowish-orange, becoming paler or whitish on the belly and underside of the throat.
It measures about 90–100 cm long and usually weighs around 13–18 kg.
Adult males have short, straight antlers without branches, unlike the Red Muntjac whose antlers have a small branch near the base.
Male Bornean Yellow Muntjacs also have enlarged upper canine teeth that curve outward from the mouth like small tusks.
Females do not have antlers; instead, they have small bony knobs with tufts of hair on their heads.
Newborn fawns have rows of white spots on their backs, and the spots remain until they grow to about half their adult size.
Unlike the Red Muntjac, the Bornean Yellow Muntjac lacks the dark eyebrow-like frontal tufts above its eyes.
It can live in moist forests, low hills, coastal areas and dense vegetation, and it is usually found relatively close to water.
Bornean Yellow Muntjacs can live in the same forests as the larger Red Muntjac, even though the two are separate species.
The Ashy Tailorbird is a very small bird, measuring about 11–11.5 cm long.
It has a grey body with a distinctive rufous-orange forehead, crown and area around the eyes.
Females are paler than males and have a white chin and throat instead of the male’s rufous-chestnut colouring.
Young Ashy Tailorbirds look different from adults: they lack the reddish colour on the head and have olive-green upperparts.
They often search for food in pairs or small family groups rather than always feeding alone.
Their food includes small insects such as ants, caterpillars, flies and beetles.
They can live in several habitats, including mangroves, coastal forests, secondary forests and even gardens.
To build its nest, the Ashy Tailorbird pierces the edges of a large leaf and “stitches” them together using plant fibres or spiderweb.
Its nest is usually built very low, no more than about 1 metre above the ground, and normally contains two or three eggs.
The Plaintive Cuckoo can lay its egg in an Ashy Tailorbird’s nest, leaving the tailorbird to care for the cuckoo chick.
A Masked Palm Civet can have a head-and-body length of about 51–76 cm, with a tail that can be almost as long as its body.
Its face has a dark mask with pale markings, including a pale stripe that can run from the nose between the eyes towards the top of the head.
Unlike many other civets, its body does not have spots or stripes, although its fur colour can range from pale brown to dark brown or reddish-brown.
It is mainly nocturnal, meaning it is most active at night.
Masked Palm Civets are good climbers but also travel on the ground, so they can move both through trees and across the forest floor.
During the day, they often sleep high in trees, and studies found that more than 80% of their daytime resting places were in trees.
Fruit makes up much of their diet, including figs, mangoes and bananas, but they can also eat small mammals, birds, frogs, snakes, snails and crabs.
When threatened, glands near the rear of the body can release a powerful-smelling secretion that helps discourage predators.
A female can have 1–4 young, and the babies open their eyes when they are about nine days old.
Masked Palm Civets help forests by spreading seeds in their droppings after eating fruit.
A leopard’s coat is covered with dark markings called rosettes because many of them look like the shape of a rose.
Some leopards have so much dark pigment that they appear almost black; these are commonly called black panthers, although their rosettes can still sometimes be seen.
Leopards are excellent climbers and can carry large prey up into trees to keep it away from scavengers such as hyenas.
They are powerful jumpers and can leap about 6 metres horizontally and around 3 metres vertically.
Leopards are also strong swimmers and may enter the water to catch animals such as fish or crabs.
They usually hunt by quietly stalking their prey and then attacking from close range rather than chasing it over long distances.
Leopards have an extremely varied diet and can hunt animals ranging from small creatures to antelopes larger than themselves.
Adult leopards usually live alone except when mating or when a mother is caring for her cubs.
A leopard’s long tail helps it balance while climbing trees and moving along branches.
Female leopards hide their cubs in safe places and may move them from one hiding spot to another while they are still young.
Its greyish-brown body usually has three dark stripes along the back, black spots on the sides, and a dark mask across the face.
Its tail is almost as long as its body and does not have rings like the tails of some other mammals.
It is mainly nocturnal, meaning it is most active at night.
It is a skilled climber and spends much of its time in trees and other high places.
