Adult Common Palm Civets usually live alone rather than travelling in groups.
Fruit forms an important part of its diet, but it also eats insects and small animals.
It is particularly attracted to fruits such as mangoes, and in Singapore it commonly eats Fishtail Palm fruits.
It can adapt to living close to people and may even use the roof spaces of buildings as shelter.
When threatened or upset, scent glands near its rear can release a very strong-smelling secretion as a chemical defence.
It can rest or raise its young inside hollow trees; litters of two or three young have been reported.
The Marbled Cat is about the size of a large domestic cat, with a head-and-body length of up to about 53 cm and a weight of up to about 5 kg.
Its thick, bushy tail can be as long as its head and body, helping it balance when moving through trees.
Its coat has large, dark-edged blotches and wavy markings that create the “marbled” pattern that gives the cat its name.
The cat has black stripes on its head, neck and back, while its legs, belly and tail have solid dark spots.
Its paws have webbing between the toes, and its claws can be completely drawn back into protective sheaths.
Although Marbled Cats are excellent climbers, recent observations suggest they spend much of their activity on the ground and are mainly active during the daytime.
They hunt small animals such as squirrels, rats and birds, and may also eat reptiles and large insects.
They live mainly in primary and tall secondary forests, from lowlands into lower mountain areas.
Marbled Cats have been recorded from sea level up to about 2,500 metres above sea level.
The Marbled Cat is closely related to the Asian Golden Cat and Borneo Bay Cat; their evolutionary branch separated from other cats millions of years ago.
The Banded Leaf Monkey is found naturally only in Singapore and southern Peninsular Malaysia.
Its body can grow to about 59 cm long, while its tail can reach about 76 cm—longer than its body.
Adults have dark grey-brown to almost black fur, with a paler underside, pale lips and white fur on the inner thighs.
Baby Banded Leaf Monkeys can have striking white or beige fur, making them look very different from the dark-coloured adults.
They are active during the daytime, especially in the morning and late afternoon.
They spend most of their time in trees and can leap across gaps between trees.
Their diet includes young leaves and forest fruits.
They usually live in small troops of up to about five or six individuals, although adult males may sometimes live alone.
When danger approaches, a male can warn the group with a loud repeated “chi-chi-chi” alarm call, causing the troop to move away.
They can live in primary forest, mature secondary forest and swamp forest.
The White-fronted Langur is found only on the island of Borneo, including parts of Malaysia and Indonesia.
It gets its name from the distinctive white, roughly diamond-shaped patch on its forehead, which contrasts with its dark head and crest.
Its tail is longer than its body: males have tails about 70–74 cm long while their bodies are about 50–54 cm long.
Its long tail helps it balance while walking along branches and leaping across gaps between trees.
It mainly eats young leaves because they are softer and easier to digest than mature leaves, but it also eats shoots and fruits.
It has a multi-chambered stomach and specialised gut bacteria that help break down the tough cellulose in leaves.
White-fronted Langurs have been observed eating soil from termite mounds, possibly to obtain minerals such as calcium, iron and salt.
They are active during the day and spend most of their time in trees, but may come down to the forest floor when gaps between trees are too large to cross.
When threatened, they may freeze quietly, gradually move lower through the trees and then escape through dense vegetation on the ground.
Unlike many langurs that make loud calls, White-fronted Langurs are relatively quiet and use soft vocalisations, even sometimes communicating softly at night.
Hose’s Langur is found only on Borneo, including parts of Sarawak and Sabah in Malaysia, Brunei, and East Kalimantan in Indonesia.
It has mostly grey fur, white tufts around its head and face, and darker black fur on its face, hands, feet and back.
It spends most of its time high in trees, especially around the middle of the forest canopy about 20 metres above the ground.
Hose’s Langurs are active during the daytime and sleep at night.
They mainly eat young leaves because these contain fewer tannins and are easier to digest, but they also eat fruits, seeds and flowers.
Their long, multi-chambered stomach helps them digest tough leaves and gives them a noticeable pot-bellied appearance.
They sometimes climb down from the trees to eat mineral-rich mud near salt springs.
They usually live in groups averaging about six individuals, although groups of up to 11 have been recorded.
A group may use a home range of about 35 hectares and travel around 740 metres in a single day.
They communicate in several ways: males use special calls to warn rival groups away, both sexes grunt when danger is nearby, and females can make chirping sounds during friendly social contact.
The Yellow-handed Mitered Langur is found naturally only on Sumatra and the nearby island of Pini in Indonesia.
Its arms, legs, tail and the top of its head can range from pale buttery yellow to bronze, while its back is usually darker brown.
It has white fur on its belly and inner thighs that extends towards the neck like a white collar, while the top of its head forms a distinctive black point.
Its face is black but is surrounded by contrasting pale pink rings around the eyes.
It mainly eats leaves, but it also feeds on fruits, flowers and seeds.
Its multi-chambered stomach contains special bacteria that help break down the tough cellulose found in leaves.
It spends most of its time in trees and uses its long arms and legs to leap, swing and run through forest branches.
It is active during the daytime and sleeps at night in particular sleeping trees.
Groups usually contain about 2–8 individuals, typically with one adult male, several females and their young.
They communicate mainly with sounds: their calls can warn others of danger or show dominance, and males give loud calls when meeting other groups.
A Maroon Surili can have a head-and-body length of up to about 58 cm.
Its tail can reach about 80 cm long, making the tail noticeably longer than its body.
Adults usually have reddish-maroon fur covering their body and tail, with grey to bluish-grey facial skin and pale lower lips.
Babies look very different from adults: they are born with creamy or buff-coloured fur, which gradually becomes reddish as they grow.
Their food includes fresh leaves, seeds, fruits and flowers.
Some populations specialise in eating large, dry forest seeds and switch to young leaves, flowers and fleshy fruits when those seeds are unavailable.
They have been seen eating soil from termite mounds in trees, possibly to obtain minerals or help reduce stomach acidity.
They can live in both primary and secondary forests and can also adapt reasonably well to regenerating forests that have previously been logged.
Maroon Surilis can live from lowland forests up to elevations of around 2,000 metres.
They are widespread across Borneo, occurring in Sabah and Sarawak in Malaysia, Brunei and Kalimantan in Indonesia.
The Black Giant Squirrel is one of the largest squirrels in the world, with a body up to about 40 cm long and a tail that can reach about 50 cm.
Its upper body and bushy tail are usually deep brown or black, while its cheeks, chest and underparts are much paler, ranging from cream to orange.
Unlike many squirrels whose tails curl over their backs, the Black Giant Squirrel’s long tail usually hangs behind it.
It spends most of its life high in the forest canopy and rarely comes down to the ground.
Despite its large size, it can make impressive leaps from branch to branch high in the trees.
It is active during the daytime and usually lives alone, although pairs or small groups may sometimes be seen during the breeding season.
Its diet includes fruits, seeds and young leaves, but it may also eat insects and occasionally bird eggs.
It builds a large, round nest from leaves and twigs high in the tree canopy; one nest in Penang was estimated to be about 80 cm across.
A female usually gives birth to only one or two young, which are nursed for about five weeks.
By eating fruits and nuts and carrying their seeds, Black Giant Squirrels help spread the seeds of forest trees.
The Tufted Ground Squirrel is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
Its body measures about 33.5–35.2 cm long, while its tail is about 29.9–34.2 cm long.
Its front teeth are unusual because each incisor has about 7–10 grooves running lengthwise along it.
Its skull is longer and flatter than the skulls of most other squirrels.
It has very hairy ears with large reddish to dark-brown tufts.
A pale stripe, ranging from white to yellowish, runs along each side of its reddish-brown body.
Its enormous fluffy tail has the largest known tail-to-body volume ratio of any mammal. The tail’s volume can be about 130% of the volume of its body.
Scientists are still unsure why its tail is so huge; ideas include distracting predators or helping the squirrels communicate or attract mates.
It searches for food mainly on the forest floor and lower parts of the forest, but it can also climb high into trees. It appears to be active during the daytime.
The Tufted Ground Squirrel mainly lives on hillsides in lowland primary forest below about 1,100 metres, although it has occasionally been seen in orchards and secondary forest.
A Shrew-faced Squirrel weighs about 187–255 g.
Its head and body are about 23 cm long, while its bushy tail is about 17 cm long.
Its fur is brown on the upper body and pale buff to white underneath.
Its long, pointed snout makes it look similar to a Common Treeshrew, but the squirrel has a shorter mouth opening and a shorter, bushier tail.
Unlike many squirrels that spend much of their time in trees, the Shrew-faced Squirrel mainly lives and searches for food on the forest floor.
It is a secretive squirrel that is rarely seen in the wild.
It is most active around early morning and late afternoon, a behaviour known as being crepuscular.
Its food includes ants, termites, earthworms and beetles.
It has unusually small upper front teeth and a very long tongue, which help it feed on insects and other small creatures.
It lives in forests across Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo, with records also from Singapore and southern Thailand.
The Sunda Pied Fantail is a small bird, measuring about 17.5–19.5 cm long.
It has a blackish head, a small white eyebrow, a white throat, a black band across the chest, greyish-brown upperparts and a white belly.
Its dark tail has broad white tips on the outer feathers, while the four feathers in the centre do not have white tips.
It is a very active bird that frequently bobs and spreads its tail into a fan while moving around.
It catches insects by suddenly flying out from a perch to grab them, a hunting technique known as “sallying.”
Sunda Pied Fantails sometimes join mixed-species feeding flocks and search for food alongside other insect-eating birds.
They sometimes follow large mammals and catch insects that are disturbed and flushed out as the mammals move.
Their song is a very high-pitched series of squeaky notes, and they can also make harsh churring and squeaky chattering calls.
They can live in forests, gardens, scrubland and mangroves, and are often found near water.
They build a cup-shaped nest from grasses and plant fibres, using spiderweb to hold the materials together.
An Indomalayan Bamboo Rat can grow about 30–45 cm long, with a tail around 20 cm long, and can weigh about 1–3 kg.
It is larger than the other species in the genus Rhizomys and also has a proportionally longer tail.
It has a distinctive triangular patch of dark fur on the top of its head.
Its short tail is only sparsely covered with hair and has soft, wrinkled skin rather than scales.
It has a broad head, a plump body, short legs and strong claws that suit a ground-dwelling lifestyle.
Its natural food includes bamboo shoots, roots and other underground parts of plants.
It may also feed on crops such as tapioca and sugarcane.
A female can have a litter of about 3–5 young after a pregnancy lasting at least 22 days.
The babies begin growing fur when they are about 10–13 days old and open their eyes at around 24 days old.
Young bamboo rats may continue nursing for 1–3 months, and individuals kept in captivity have lived for about four years.
A Northern Treeshrew’s head and body measure about 14–23 cm long, and its tail is roughly the same length as its body.
It has greyish-olive fur, a long pointed snout and a bushy tail, giving it a squirrel-like appearance even though it is not a squirrel.
Northern Treeshrews are active during the daytime and are usually found on or near the ground, although they climb trees more often when food on the forest floor becomes scarce.
They mark their territories using scent glands on their abdomen and chin.
Their wild diet consists mainly of insects, especially beetles, along with fruit.
Northern Treeshrews have been shown to willingly eat spicy foods because a genetic change makes them much less sensitive to capsaicin, the chemical that makes chilli peppers feel hot.
Their body temperature can change from about 35°C at night to about 40°C during the day.
They can make at least eight different types of sounds, including calls used for alarm, attention, contact and defence.
Northern Treeshrews have an unusual relationship with pitcher plants: they lick nectar from the plant and leave droppings inside the pitcher, which the plant uses as nutrients.
Mothers usually have two babies and show unusual parenting: they may visit the young only once every two days to nurse them for about five minutes.
The Common Treeshrew is one of the larger treeshrews, with a body about 16–21 cm long and an average weight of around 190 g. Its bushy tail is almost as long as its body.
Its fur can vary from reddish-brown to greyish or dark brown, but it usually has a narrow pale stripe on each shoulder.
It is active during the daytime and spends much of its time searching for food on the forest floor or among low vegetation and fallen branches.
Common Treeshrews move quickly through the forest undergrowth with short, jerky movements while searching for food.
They are omnivores that eat insects, fruit and leaves, and they have even been observed eating small vertebrates.
When hunting, they often use their long snout to capture prey, but they can use their front paws to grab flying insects or food that is just out of reach.
When eating fruit, they can discard much of the fibre before swallowing it, helping the fruit pass through their digestive system more quickly.
They communicate using scent by rubbing glands on their chest and abdomen against objects, and they can also mark their territory with urine and droppings.
A family can share and defend the same home range, but individuals usually spread out and search for food independently during the day.
Baby Common Treeshrews are born very underdeveloped: their eyes begin opening at about 20 days old, and they can leave the nest at around 36 days old.
The Large Treeshrew is native to Sumatra and nearby islands, as well as the lowlands and hills of Borneo.
It averages about 22 cm in head-and-body length and weighs around 198 g, with an unusually long snout compared with other treeshrews.
Its dark brown back has a black stripe running down the middle, while each shoulder has a yellow stripe and its underside is reddish-orange.
It is the most ground-dwelling of all treeshrew species and spends most of its foraging time on the forest floor.
Large Treeshrews are active during the daytime and usually live alone rather than travelling in groups.
They use their claws to dig beneath the top layer of soil and their long snouts to search for foods such as earthworms, centipedes, millipedes and beetle larvae.
When eating fruit, they may suck out the juice and spit out tough fibres, seeds and other plant material instead of swallowing everything.
They mark their territories with scents produced by glands on their chin and near their rear.
They use different alarm sounds depending on distance: they may chatter when danger is close but whistle when danger is farther away.
Mothers have an unusual parenting style: they may visit their babies only every other day and nurse them for less than five minutes at a time.
The Roughneck Monitor can grow to about 1.3–1.5 metres in total length.
It gets its name from the large, pointed scales on the back of its neck, which have strong raised ridges.
It has a long, pointed snout and a strong ridge above each eye.
Adults are mainly dark grey with yellowish bands and markings, while young Roughneck Monitors usually have much stronger patterns.
Its tail can be about 1.6 times as long as the distance from its snout to the base of its tail.
It can move both on the forest floor and in trees, and has been seen on fallen logs and climbing tree trunks.
It often shelters inside holes in trees when it needs a hiding place.
When threatened, it may escape, puff up its throat, release urine or droppings, or even close its eyes and stay still as if playing dead.
Its diet can include ants, termites, centipedes, stick insects, cockroaches, spiders, scorpions, frogs and crabs.
Females can lay about 8–16 eggs in a clutch, and the eggs may take roughly 152–190 days to hatch.
A water monitor can stay submerged for 30 minutes. These super swimmers can handle rivers and even salty seawater.
The common water monitor uses its long, powerful, flattened tail like a swimming tool, helping the common water monitor move and steer through the water.
The common water monitor is a carnivore and scavenger with a huge menu, from fish and crabs to snakes and even crocodile eggs. The common water monitor can also smell carrion from far away.
Most adult common water monitors are around 1.5 to 2 m long, but exceptional common water monitors can become enormous. One reported record individual measured 3.21 m.
A common water monitor's pattern changes as it grows up. Young ones can show brighter yellow spots, but those markings gradually fade with age.
A female common water monitor can lay around 20 to 50 eggs. Common water monitor eggs may be hidden in termite mounds, rotten wood, or burrows and take about 5 to 6 months to hatch.
Male common water monitors can be very territorial and may fight rival males with powerful bites.
The common water monitor uses a forked tongue to help pinpoint where smells are coming from while searching for food.
Male common water monitors can become reproductively mature at about 40 cm and 1 kg, while females reach maturity at about 50 cm. Common water monitors keep growing well beyond those sizes.
A common water monitor comes with three built-in defense tools, a whipping tail, sharp claws, and a strong bite.
The green-billed coucal is found naturally only in Sri Lanka's wet zone, so the green-billed coucal is not a Malaysian native species.
The green-billed coucal is a fairly large bird, about 43 to 45 cm long, with dark glossy plumage, reddish wings, a long greenish tail, and a pale green bill.
The green-billed coucal's bill is normally pale green, but the green-billed coucal's bill can turn ivory during the breeding season.
Mum and dad green-billed coucals can be hard to tell apart, but youngsters give away their age with duller, streakier feathers and greyish eyes.
The green-billed coucal eats a varied animal diet that includes insects, caterpillars, small vertebrates, spiders, and lizards, with snails being a particular favourite.
This bird likes to hunt low and sneaky. The green-billed coucal pushes through leaves and tangled plants on the forest floor looking for its next meal.
The green-billed coucal is a secretive forest bird that hides in thick vegetation, so hearing the green-billed coucal is often easier than seeing it.

The green-billed coucal builds a concealed domed nest in thick vegetation. Green-billed coucal nests have been described about 1.2 to 1.5 metres above the ground, with a typical clutch of 2 to 3 eggs.
The green-billed coucal is believed to breed from January through July, and the green-billed coucal lays chalky white eggs measuring about 34.7 by 27 mm.
The green-billed coucal gives a deep, booming call of usually two or three syllables. Male green-billed coucals call more often than females, especially during the breeding season.
Greater coucal pairs can defend surprisingly large nesting territories. In one southern Indian study, greater coucal territories ranged from 0.9 to 7.2 hectares.
The greater coucal hides its domed nest in thick vegetation, and greater coucal nests can be positioned up to 6 metres above the ground.
With shiny black feathers, brown wings, a super-long tail, and ruby-red eyes, the greater coucal looks dramatic. The females are even a little bigger than the males.
Greater coucal eggs start out chalky white with a yellowish glaze, but the greater coucal's egg colour changes as that outer coating gradually wears off.
Female greater coucals are larger than males. Female greater coucals weigh about 275 to 380 g, compared with about 208 to 270 g for males.
This bird can stomach some surprising food. Greater coucals have been seen eating poisonous yellow oleander fruit, and they sometimes snack on ripe oil palm fruit too.
Greater coucal babies grow fast. The eggs hatch after only about 15 to 16 days, and the youngsters can leave the nest about 18 to 22 days later.
Greater coucals can sing a duet. When a pair calls together, the female has the deeper voice. They can also rattle, scold, and even hiss.
A male greater coucal brings food to the female during courtship and does most of the work building their nest. The greater coucal's nest can take about 3 to 8 days to construct.

The greater coucal's deep call can carry a long way, especially around dawn and dusk. In some cultures, the greater coucal's call is linked with approaching rain, which has earned it the nickname "rain crow."
It is nicknamed the "whistling dog" because it uses high-pitched whistles to communicate with other pack members.
Raising baby dholes takes a whole team. Pack members babysit, guard the den, and even bring back food for the pups.
Teamwork makes these hunters powerful. A dhole pack can tackle an animal weighing more than 10 times as much as one dhole.
Dholes can run a relay race while hunting. One group chases hard, then other packmates can take over when the first hunters get tired.
A dhole has quite the sound effects collection. It can whistle, yip, mew, scream, and even make a sound a bit like a chicken clucking.
Dinner rule in a dhole pack: kids first. When pups become old enough to join hunts, the grown-ups let them eat before everyone else.
Dholes usually hunt when the sun is up, but a bright moon can sometimes tempt them out for a nighttime hunt.
The dhole has an unusual dental feature, the dhole has one fewer lower molar on each side than many other canids.
Dhole pups do not become hunters right away. At about 10 weeks they start exploring outside the den, then around 6 to 7 months they can join the pack on hunts.
Malaysia is one of the countries where dholes still live in the wild today but it is so rare and hard to spot!
An Otter Civet can grow up to about 68 cm in head-and-body length and weigh up to about 5 kg.
Its feet are partly webbed, helping it move through the water as part of its semi-aquatic lifestyle.
It can close both its nostrils and its ears when it goes underwater.
It has a broad muzzle, white lips and many unusually long whiskers that may help it find food.
Otter Civets are nocturnal, meaning they are active mainly at night.
Despite being adapted to water, the Otter Civet is also a surprisingly good climber and can climb trees.
It mainly lives around rivers, streams and swamp forests and usually stays close to water.
Its food includes aquatic animals such as fish, crabs and freshwater molluscs, but it may also eat birds and small mammals.
When walking, it often keeps its head and tail low while holding its back in an arched position.
Female Otter Civets generally have two or three young, and newborns do not yet have the frosted grey hairs seen on adults.
This small fruit bat weighs about 32–42 g, with a forearm measuring about 59–70 mm.
It gets the name “dog-faced” from its short, dog-like snout, and its large eyes help it see well at night.
The edges of its ears and the bones in its wings are usually white; adult males also tend to have a reddish-orange neck collar, while females are more yellowish.
It usually becomes active around dusk or just after sunset, when it flies out to look for fruiting trees.
During the day, these bats often rest upside down in small groups beneath palm leaves, among foliage or on tree branches.
A male may spend more than two months chewing the veins of leaves and palm fronds so that they collapse into an umbrella-like shelter for his group.
Its diet is mainly fruit, including figs, bananas, guavas and mangoes, but it can also feed on nectar and pollen.
After choosing a fruit from a tree, it may carry the fruit to a quiet feeding spot before eating the soft pulp.
In Peninsular Malaysia, females can breed throughout the year and usually have one baby, which the mother carries when it is young and nurses for about 6–8 weeks.
By feeding on fruits, nectar and pollen, these bats help plants by spreading seeds and contributing to pollination.
The Black-rumped Flameback is about 26–29 cm long.
It has bright golden-yellow wings, a black rump and throat, and whitish underparts covered with dark chevron-shaped markings.
Males have a bright red crown and crest, while females have a black-and-white crown with red mainly on the crest.
It has a loud rattling or chattering call and flies in an undulating, wave-like pattern.
Black-rumped Flamebacks are often seen in pairs or small groups and sometimes join mixed-species flocks while searching for food.
They search for food from the forest floor all the way up to the tree canopy.
They use their strong bills to reach beetle larvae hidden beneath tree bark, and they also visit termite mounds and drink nectar.
While moving around branches, they may hop to the opposite side of a branch or trunk to hide from possible predators.
During the breeding season, usually between February and July, they frequently drum on trees with their bills.
They usually lay three glossy white eggs inside a nest cavity; the eggs hatch after about 11 days, and the chicks leave the nest about 20 days later.
Hose’s Civet is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
It can grow to about 50 cm in head-and-body length, with a tail up to about 32 cm long, and can weigh up to around 3 kg.
Its upper body is dark brown to almost black, while its belly and the inner surfaces of its legs are pale or whitish.
It has very long facial whiskers, a large flesh-coloured snout and nostrils that open widely towards the sides.
Hose’s Civets are mainly active at night but can also be active around dusk.
They appear to spend much of their time on the ground rather than high in trees.
Their feet are partly webbed, which together with their long whiskers suggests they may search for food around rocky forest streams.
They have been recorded from elevations of about 325 to 1,700 metres, including both lower and mountain forests.
Many records come from very humid forests, and researchers think they may favour places near mossy rocks and streams.
For many years scientists knew Hose’s Civet mainly from museum specimens; the first living individual studied by researchers was obtained in 1997 and later released.
The Mountain Imperial Pigeon is a large pigeon, measuring about 43–51 cm long.
It has a greyish head, neck and underparts, a contrasting white throat, and distinctive maroon-brown wings and back.
Its wings are broad and rounded, and it flies with relatively slow wingbeats.
Its call is a deep, resonant booming sound that may be difficult to hear unless the bird is fairly close.
Although usually seen alone, Mountain Imperial Pigeons can gather in groups of up to about 20 birds, especially when travelling to roosts or moving through mountains.
They spend much of their time high in the forest canopy and often fly above the treetops, which can make them difficult to spot.
They mainly eat fruits and berries, especially figs and nutmeg, which they can pluck and swallow whole.
They can live from sea level to high mountain forests, reaching about 2,550 metres in the Himalayas and about 2,200 metres on Sumatra.
During courtship, a bird puffs up its throat and bows, then flies about 6–8 metres upward before gliding back down with its wings and tail spread wide.
They build a simple platform nest about 5–8 metres above the ground, usually lay one egg, rarely two, and both parents help incubate the eggs.
You might smell a moonrat before you see one. It gives off a super-strong scent that smells a bit like ammonia.
Moonrats are nighttime explorers. When the sun comes up, they hide under logs and roots or move into an empty burrow for a daytime nap.
The moonrat has a head-and-body length of about 32 to 40 cm, plus a tail measuring another 20 to 29 cm, and the moonrat weighs roughly 870 g to 1.1 kg.
Moonrats like their personal space. They mark their territory with a powerful smell and can hiss to tell other animals, "Stay away!"
The moonrat can reproduce at any time of year. A female moonrat is pregnant for about 35 to 40 days and usually has two babies.
Plot twist, the moonrat is not a rat at all! Its relatives include hedgehogs and other animals called gymnures.
A moonrat can live for as long as about five years. That is several years of nighttime exploring, swimming, and sniffing for food.
Not every white Bornean moonrat looks exactly the same. Those in western Borneo usually have more black hairs, while eastern ones tend to look whiter.
The moonrat has unusually large hind feet, measuring about 6.5 to 7.5 cm long.
The moonrat has a built-in food detector on its face. Its long, bendy snout helps it poke through leaves and dirt to find tasty insects and worms.
The White-crowned Forktail is the largest forktail, measuring about 25–28 cm long.
It has a striking black-and-white pattern, with a white crown, white belly and rump, black throat and breast, and a bold white band across its dark wings.
Its long tail is deeply forked and patterned with black and white bands.
Young White-crowned Forktails do not yet have the adult’s bright white crown and have browner, mottled plumage.
It frequently wags its tail while moving around streams and other wet areas.
It searches along stream edges and even in the water for insects such as beetles, water crickets, springtails and caterpillars.
Its calls include high-pitched whistles, while males can produce longer songs containing whistles, clicks and bell-like sounds.
It prefers forest streams, fast-flowing rivers and waterfalls, usually in places surrounded by dense vegetation.
Its nest is a large cup made from moss, leaves, plants and wood fibres and is usually built close to or directly above water.
Some White-crowned Forktails build their nests behind waterfalls and must fly through the falling water to reach them.
The Black-crowned Pitta is a small bird, measuring about 13–15.5 cm long and weighing about 50–64 g.
Adults have a black head and breast, a brilliant crimson belly, dark purple-blue upperparts and a bright blue patch on the wings.
A narrow pale blue or silvery-blue stripe extends backwards from behind each eye.
The tip of its bill can be bright red to orange.
Young birds look very different from adults: nestlings are yellow, while juveniles become uniformly dark brown before developing their colourful adult feathers.
It is found only on Borneo and has been recorded mainly in Sabah, Malaysia.
It prefers dark, damp parts of lowland rainforest, especially shaded gullies and ravines with dense vegetation.
It mainly eats small animals without backbones, including spiders, ants, cockroaches, beetles and snails.
Its song is a clear whistle that rises in pitch and then ends abruptly.
It builds a dome-shaped nest from materials such as sticks, bark, roots and leaves, and a clutch normally contains two eggs.
The Crimson-headed Partridge is about 25 cm long; one measured adult male weighed about 330 g.
Adult males have a striking crimson-red head, neck and breast, while most of the rest of the body is dark blackish; their bill is yellow to yellowish-white.
Females are duller than males, with brownish-black plumage, a more orange-red head and breast, and a dark brownish-black bill. Females also lack the leg spurs found on males.
Young birds are much duller than adults, with the crimson colour mainly limited to the top of the head.
The species is found only on Borneo, where it mainly lives in lower montane forests in the northern and central parts of the island.
It is usually found between about 1,000 and 1,700 metres above sea level, although records range from as low as 185 m to as high as 3,050 m.
It searches on the forest floor and among short vegetation for berries, insects and even small crustaceans.
Pairs can perform loud duets, with two birds giving their harsh calls alternately to one another.
Its nest is made from dry leaves and is hidden inside clumps of grass or lichen.
A clutch can contain 8–9 light-brown eggs with darker streaks; in captivity, the eggs have taken about 18–19 days to hatch.
Its scientific name literally translates to "half weasel," describing how it looks.
Scientists searching Peninsular Malaysia a few years back only managed to find this civet in two spots, both in the hills of Terengganu.
If this civet feels threatened, it actually puffs up its tail to look bigger and scarier.
It can actually feel out its prey using extra-sensitive hairs tucked between the pads of its paws.
When hunting something bigger, it grabs the back of the neck and shakes hard, then holds its catch down with its front paws.
This civet has a close relative, Hose's civet, that looks and is built almost exactly like it.
Genetic testing shows two groups of this civet split apart from each other nearly 3 million years ago.
This civet now only occupies about a fifth of the land it used to live in, and barely a tenth of what's left is actually protected.
Count the stripes on its back, it usually has seven or eight dark bands, plus a tail that changes from brown to solid black.
It usually stays on the ground at night, but it can climb well too, and sometimes even hunts along forest streams for water creatures.
This bird was first officially described using a specimen collected right here in Malacca, Malaysia, back in 1845.
Its name literally means "ash grey" in Latin, the perfect color for blending into shady forest light.
This bird has its own Malay name too, "Merbah-Kelabu Biasa."
This bird used to be lumped together with a related species, the ashy bulbul, until scientists decided they were different enough to split into two.
Even its genus name means "half," because an early scientist thought it looked like a cross between two other bird groups.
The Borneo version of this bird has a splash of yellow-green on its wings that the mainland Malaysian version doesn't have at all.
This bird is so light it weighs about as much as a small egg.
This bird loves company, it often gathers with other bulbul species at fruit trees for a group feast.
This bird prefers hilly, mountain forests, though every so often it turns up down in the lowlands too.
This bird has been heard calling almost at sea level and also way up at 1,650 metres in the mountains of Sarawak.
Look closely at this mongoose's fur and you may spot tiny golden or reddish flecks. That is why auropunctata means "gold-spotted."
Mongoose super-size trick! When facing danger, the small Indian mongoose can puff up its fur and look about twice its normal size.
A small Indian mongoose cannot tuck away its claws like a cat. Its long claws stay out all the time, and each foot has five toes.
This mongoose has its own natural heating and cooling system. It can sunbathe on chilly mornings, then scrape away hot dirt to find a cooler spot when the day gets too warm.
This mongoose does not win snake battles by being magically poison-proof. Its secret weapon is speed, dodging strikes and attacking quickly around the snake's head.
A mongoose has about 12 different calls, including a high-pitched mating sound that sounds like "giggling."
Baby mongooses arrive fast. Pregnancy lasts only about 49 days, and there may be up to five pups. Boys can mature at about 122 days, while girls take around 301 days.
The small Indian mongoose was deliberately introduced to islands to control rats, but small Indian mongooses also attacked native wildlife and became invasive predators.
Mongooses can have playtime too. In captivity they have been seen playing and grooming each other, while wild mums may groom their babies.
This mongoose usually likes being alone, but breeding season can change the rules. Some males have been seen hanging out together and even sharing a burrow.
Where a short-tailed mongoose lives makes a big difference. On the mainland it is mostly found below about 100 m, but on Borneo it can climb to around 1,500 m or even higher.
These mongooses need lots of space. In a Malaysian study, males roamed across an average area of 233 hectares, much larger than the females' 132 hectares.
Short-tailed mongooses like their personal space. They normally travel alone and keep territories of their own.
Its name is not kidding. The short-tailed mongoose has a tail only a little more than half as long as its head and body together.
Not every short-tailed mongoose wears exactly the same coat. Some look nearly black, while others are browner or reddish, and their faces can have lighter and darker patches.
This mongoose may be called short-tailed, but the whole animal can still reach around 60 to 65 cm long. Some can weigh as much as about 2 kg.
The short-tailed mongoose uses sensitive whiskers to help the short-tailed mongoose detect nearby objects and prey while moving through thick vegetation.
A short-tailed mongoose can leave a smelly message instead of a sign. Its scent marks tell other mongooses, "Someone lives here."
Baby short-tailed mongooses need lots of help from Mum. After about 60 to 70 days of pregnancy, she usually has 1 to 4 babies, and they take around 1 to 2 years to grow into breeding adults.
The short-tailed mongoose has a chunky-looking face, with a broad snout and small round ears that make it look extra tough.
Scientists don't fully agree on whether this mongoose is more of a nighttime or daytime hunter!
Genetic testing in 2009 was enough to move this mongoose into a whole new scientific genus
Look closely and you might spot two different color types of this mongoose, mostly brown, but sometimes a rarer reddish version.
Even though an ocean separates them, the mongooses on Borneo and Sumatra are genetically almost identical.

Mongoose populations on Palawan Island in the southern Philippines, previously classified as a different species, are now considered by some researchers to actually be a form of the Collared Mongoose.
Even though it usually lives alone, camera traps have often caught pairs of these mongooses together.
This mongoose used to be so poorly studied that scientists couldn't even rate how threatened it was, until a 2015 review found it Near Threatened.
This mongoose has been photographed living in a logged forest reserve in Sabah, Borneo.
It can cope with a somewhat damaged forest, but once the land becomes a farm, this mongoose mostly disappears.
This mongoose can live from the flat lowlands all the way up to nearly 1,400 metres in the hills.
This gibbon actually picks the tallest trees on hilltops to call from, since it helps its voice travel further through the forest.
It has special built-in cushions on its bottom, hard bony pads that make sitting on branches more comfortable.
No other gibbon species is spread across such a huge north-to-south range as this one.
A mother gibbon usually only has one baby every three and a half years, a very slow pace for having young.
This gibbon can live for up to 30 years out in the wild.
When a gibbon pair sings together in the morning, their duet can be heard almost a kilometre away through the forest.
Even without a tail to help balance, this gibbon can actually walk upright along branches high in the trees.
Two gibbons from the very same family group can have totally different coat colors, anywhere from dark brown to cream.
Sadly, baby gibbons have sometimes been taken for the pet trade by hunters who shoot the mother first, which is one reason this species needs protecting.
This gibbon eats lots of different plants, but figs seem to be one of its favorite treats.
The Malayan Porcupine is one of the largest porcupines in Southeast Asia, with a head-and-body length of up to about 72 cm.
Its quills are actually modified hairs. The long quills on its back are usually black-and-white or dark-brown-and-white, while young porcupines are born with softer quills that harden as they grow.
Its short tail has thick, hollow quills that it can shake to make a rattling sound when it feels threatened.
Its short tail has thick, hollow quills that it can shake to make a rattling sound when it feels threatened.
They eat fallen fruits, roots, tubers and bark, and their powerful jaws can crush hard seeds and nuts. They are even known to gnaw on bones and carry them back to their burrows.
They dig large burrows using their powerful front feet and long claws. These burrows can form extensive tunnel systems and may be used by many generations.
Family bonds can be strong: groups of 2–4 Malayan Porcupines may forage together at night, and as many as 10 can live in the same colony.
When seriously threatened, a Malayan Porcupine can raise its quills and charge backwards toward an attacker, using its sharp spines for defence.
Despite their heavy, spiny bodies, Malayan Porcupines are able to swim.
A female usually gives birth to one pup after a pregnancy of about 90–112 days, although twins have also been recorded.
The Four-striped Ground Squirrel is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
It belongs to the squirrel family Sciuridae, the same family that contains tree squirrels, ground squirrels and flying squirrels.
Its scientific name is Lariscus hosei, and it belongs to a group known as the striped ground squirrels.
As its common name suggests, the Four-striped Ground Squirrel is recognised by four stripes running along its back.
Its natural habitat includes subtropical and tropical dry forests on Borneo.
The genus Lariscus contains four recognised species of striped ground squirrels.
All members of the genus Lariscus occur naturally in Southeast Asia.
The species was scientifically described by British zoologist Oldfield Thomas in 1892.
When it was first scientifically described, it was called Sciurus hosei rather than Lariscus hosei.
Habitat loss is recognised as a threat to the Four-striped Ground Squirrel because it depends on forest habitat.
The Three-striped Ground Squirrel has a head-and-body length of about 23 cm, with a shorter tail of about 14 cm.
Its upper body and tail range from deep brown to orange-brown, while its underside is much paler.
It is easy to recognise by three thick black stripes that run from its shoulders to the base of its tail.
It is active during the daytime and spends almost all of its time on the ground.
Even when crossing fallen trees, it rarely climbs more than about one metre above the ground.
It digs through loose surface soil while searching for food such as roots, fallen fruits and insects.
Its nests are usually hidden inside the rotting trunks of fallen trees.
It is a shy, nervous squirrel that quickly runs into the forest to hide when disturbed.
Its alarm calls can sound like a repeated “chi-it” or a descending “phe-ew”, and it may flick its tail while calling.
Its range stretches from southern Thailand through Peninsular Malaysia to Sumatra, Java and Borneo.
A noisy rat's wild life is fairly short. The supplied source gives its typical natural lifespan as about three years.
No eggs for this rat. Baby noisy rats develop inside their mum before being born alive.
The noisy rat likes the in-between hours. Instead of choosing bright daytime or deep nighttime, it is especially active around sunrise and sunset.
Scientists tracked these rats with radio equipment and found their movements could cover areas from roughly 2,083 to 9,829 square metres.
This rat has a seriously long tail. Its body can be about 27 cm long, but its tail can stretch to around 41 cm.
A long-tailed giant rat can weigh about 500 g, roughly half a kilogram. That is pretty hefty for a forest rat.
The long-tailed giant rat usually lives below about 1,200 m, but an exceptional record from Mount Kinabalu reached around 3,100 m.
This rat has a two-tone coat. The long-tailed giant rat is dark and golden-brown on top, but much paler underneath.
Look closely at the tail. The back half is usually pale, and instead of fluffy fur, the tail is scaly with tiny bristles.
This rat can go vertical. The long-tailed giant rat usually stays near the ground, but it can climb surprisingly high into the trees.
The White-tailed Wattled Pheasant is found naturally only on the island of Borneo.
Adult males can reach about 80 cm long, while females are smaller at about 55 cm.
Males have mostly glossy black plumage, a maroon breast, bright red legs and a huge fan of pure white tail feathers.
Females look very different from males: they are mostly rufous-brown and have a much shorter, narrower tail.
Both males and females have bright blue facial skin, but males have large blue wattles that can expand during display.
During courtship, a male can spread his enormous white tail into a dramatic fan and raise his blue facial wattles.
It lives mainly in hilly foothill and lower montane rainforest and is rarely found in lowlands below about 300 metres.
These pheasants may move around the forest to search for trees that are producing fruit.
Their diet includes fruits as well as worms and insects.
The species was named after Sir Henry Ernest Gascoyne Bulwer, who presented the first scientific specimen to the British Museum.
The Rufous-tailed Fantail is found naturally only on the island of Java in Indonesia.
It lives in subtropical or tropical moist mountain forests.
Its reddish-brown, or rufous, tail helps distinguish it from the other two fantail species found on Java.
It has a noticeable white throat.
Its facial markings form distinctive eyebrow-like markings that eBird describes as giving it an “angry” appearance.
It is an active bird that lives in foothill and mountain forests.
Rufous-tailed Fantails often travel and forage together with mixed-species bird flocks.
They often move through tangled vegetation in the lower and middle levels of the forest rather than staying high in the canopy.
Their song is a squeaky series of notes that repeatedly move up and down in pitch.
Their call is a short, dry sound described as “chrit.”
This bird was only officially recognized as its own separate species in 2023, before that it was lumped together with a related fireback from Borneo.
The Malayan Crested Fireback is distinguished from the closely related Bornean crested fireback by its white central tail feathers, red legs, and bluish black plumage streaked with white below.
There's a mysterious population in Sumatra that scientists now believe is actually a natural mix between this bird and its close relative in Borneo.

Male Malayan Crested Firebacks display a peacock-like dark crest, glossy blue-black plumage, a reddish brown rump, and bare blue facial skin that enlarges into wattles, while shorter-crested females are brown with black and white spotted underparts.
This bird likes to live near rivers, especially spots that flood sometimes, and mostly stays down low rather than up in the mountains.
The Malayan Crested Fireback feeds in groups of up to six birds, more often outside the breeding season, on a diet of berries, fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates.
The Malayan Crested Fireback is most frequently heard vocalizing in the early morning and late afternoon.
This bird has been photographed right here in Malaysia, in Taman Negara National Park.
This bird is considered Vulnerable, meaning its home forests and hunting pressure are putting it at real risk.
Its scientific name literally means "red," describing the reddish patch of feathers on its lower back.
Malay crested firebacks occur on the Thai-Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, including Taman Negara.
Malay crested firebacks make their homes in lowland rainforests, especially wetter places!
The Malay crested fireback can grow up to 70 cm long.
Malay crested fireback males wear blue-black feathers with reddish-brown rumps; females wear brown!
A male Malay crested fireback’s tail mixes colours: white in the middle and black outside!
Malay crested firebacks explore the forest floor for food, solo or with a small group!
Listen for a Malay crested fireback calling “chuckit” or a softer “weep”!
Male Malay crested firebacks perform displays that produce whirring wing sounds.
Malay crested firebacks have blue facial skin and red legs; Malayan crestless firebacks have red facial skin and grey legs.
Malay crested firebacks need safe forest homes, because forest loss and too much hunting threaten these birds!
Smooth-coated otters have been spotted in Malaysian places such as Ipoh and Penang!
The smooth-coated otter has short, smooth fur and a hairless nose.
Smooth-coated otters have large, webbed feet and flattened tails.
Smooth-coated otters eat fish, shellfish and crustaceans.
Smooth-coated otters use sensitive whiskers to detect disturbances in water.
Some smooth-coated otters build burrows with underwater entrances leading to chambers above the high-water line.
Smooth-coated otters at Kuala Selangor Nature Park were observed hunting fish in a slightly V-shaped formation.
Smooth-coated otters observed in Peninsular Malaysia were mainly active by day and rested briefly around midday.
Smooth-coated otters can visit salty coastal waters, but freshwater must still be nearby!
Smooth-coated otters have several possible family sizes: sources report 1–2 or 2–5 babies per litter!
Perlis State Park is a Malaysian home for stump-tailed macaques!
A stump-tailed macaque has a tiny tail, only 3.2–6.9 cm long!
Baby stump-tailed macaques have white fur, while adults usually have dark fur.
Stump-tailed macaques store food briefly in cheek pouches.
The stump-tailed macaque’s pink or red face becomes darker with age.
Stump-tailed macaques spend most of their time on the ground but can climb trees.
Stump-tailed macaques typically live in groups of 10–60, including several adult males and females.
About 50 stump-tailed macaques were observed visiting a Perlis oil-palm plantation early in the morning.
Male and female stump-tailed macaques can become partly bald as they age.
Stump-tailed macaques are protected under Malaysia’s Wildlife Conservation Act 2010
Southern red muntjacs live in both Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo!
A barking animal might be a southern red muntjac warning of danger!
Male southern red muntjacs wear short antlers raised on bony stalks!
Male southern red muntjacs leave scent messages to mark their territory!
Southern red muntjacs enjoy a forest menu of leaves, shoots, bark, grass and fallen fruit!
Young southern red muntjacs sometimes have white spots.
Male southern red muntjacs have another weapon besides antlers: long upper canine teeth!
Cameras have spotted southern red muntjacs in young acacia plantations in Bintulu, Sarawak!
A southern red muntjac mother usually has one baby after 6–7 months, but sometimes has twins!
A grown southern red muntjac can weigh 13–35 kg.
Malaysia shares the Malayan weasel with neighbouring parts of Southeast Asia!
Malayan weasels come in several colours, from golden shades to pale greyish-white!
A Malayan weasel’s head and body are about a school ruler long, or slightly longer!
A Malayan weasel’s long body helps the hunter follow animals into underground burrows!
Malayan weasels live in several settings, including forests and grassy places!
Malayan weasels have been found high in the mountains, up to 1,700 metres
Malayan weasels are usually spotted by day, but their nighttime lives need more investigation!
Spot a Malayan weasel, and the animal will probably be alone!
One recorded Malayan weasel family had four babies in a single litter!
Cameras found Malayan weasels in both original forest and forest where trees had been cut, at heights of 177–1,032 metres!
Sunda stink badgers live in Sabah’s lowlands too, with records just 10 metres above sea level!
The Sunda stink badger has a surprising family connection: skunks!
Sunda stink badgers do not all have the same stripe: some white stripes have gaps!
A threatened Sunda stink badger raises the tail and releases a foul-smelling secretion.
Sunda stink badgers usually forage at night and rest in burrows by day.
Sunda stink badgers search soil for food using their snouts and strong front claws.
Sunda stink badgers can conceal burrow entrances using twigs and dry leaves.
Sunda stink badgers eat plants as well as worms, insects and bird eggs.
Sunda stink badgers have been reported to produce two or three young per litter
The Sunda stink badger has a short tail, reported as about 3.6 cm or 5–7.5 cm.
Sunda clouded leopards live on Borneo and Sumatra, including Malaysia’s Sabah and Sarawak.
The Sunda clouded leopard is the largest wild cat species on Borneo.
The Sunda clouded leopard gets its name from cloud-like coat markings containing smaller spots.
The Sunda clouded leopard’s tail can match the body in length and helps with balance.
Sunda clouded leopards have canine teeth about 5.1 cm long, proportionally longer than those of any other living cat.
Sunda clouded leopards can climb headfirst down tree trunks using flexible hind-leg joints.
Sunda clouded leopards hunt mammals including porcupines, civets, deer and pigs.
Researchers identified four Sunda clouded leopards from their tracks during a 2005 study in Tabin Wildlife Reserve.
Sunda clouded leopards can survive in partly logged forests, although fewer generally occupy a given area.
Forest loss threatens Sunda clouded leopards by reducing living space and available prey.
The mainland clouded leopard lives in Peninsular Malaysia; Borneo has the Sunda clouded leopard.
The clouded leopard’s cloud-shaped markings help conceal the cat.
The clouded leopard uses a 61–91 cm tail for balance in trees.
The clouded leopard can climb down tree trunks headfirst.
The clouded leopard can suspend the body from branches using the hind legs.
The clouded leopard eats animals including deer, birds, monkeys and porcupines.
A photograph from northern Peninsular Malaysia caught a clouded leopard carrying a binturong!
The clouded leopard has the longest canine teeth relative to body size among living cats
Clouded leopard cubs open their eyes approximately 10 days after birth.
The clouded leopard is threatened by forest destruction and illegal hunting.
Blyth’s hawk-eagle has been recorded in Sabah and six states on the Malaysian peninsula!
Blyth’s hawk-eagle lives on both a peninsula and large Southeast Asian islands!
Blyth’s hawk-eagle is roughly half a metre long, sometimes a little more!
Adult Blyth’s hawk-eagles have a broad white tail band visible from above and below.
Young Blyth’s hawk-eagles are dark brown above, with lighter brown heads and undersides.
A Blyth’s hawk-eagle family starts with one egg in a treetop stick nest!
Blyth’s hawk-eagle can raise the crest while perched; the crest is hidden in flight.
Adult Blyth’s hawk-eagles display broad, rounded wings in flight.
Mountain forests are a place to look for Blyth’s hawk-eagle!
Young Blyth’s hawk-eagles resemble Wallace’s hawk-eagles, but size and elevation provide identification clues.
The changeable hawk-eagle has been recorded across Malaysia, including Sabah and seven states on the peninsula!
Changeable hawk-eagles can have pale or dark plumage.
The changeable hawk-eagle uses forests, their edges, large parks and plantations
A dark changeable hawk-eagle can be distinguished from dark honey-buzzards by longer wings and a slimmer profile.
A changeable hawk-eagle on the Malay Peninsula may have a tiny feather “hairstyle”, or none!
The changeable hawk-eagle has feathers covering the legs.
The changeable hawk-eagle hunts by watching from a perch and swooping onto prey.
The changeable hawk-eagle can catch prey close to the water’s surface.
Changeable hawk-eagle pairs may reuse nests, with both adults making repairs.
A mother changeable hawk-eagle spends about 40 days keeping one egg warm!
A dark-necked tailorbird was observed at the Rainforest Discovery Centre in Sepilok, Sabah.
Dark-necked tailorbirds inhabit moist lowland forests and mangrove forests.
Dark-necked tailorbirds have olive backs, pale undersides and reddish-brown crowns.
Male dark-necked tailorbirds have a dark neck patch that is sometimes hidden.
Dark-necked tailorbirds have more extensive reddish-brown crowns than common tailorbirds.
Dark-necked tailorbirds often sing trilled phrases in duets.
Dark-necked tailorbirds can be shy and remain deep within tangled vegetation.
A dark-necked tailorbird’s greenish tail is a useful identification clue in Borneo.
Dark-necked tailorbirds can look different across Malaysia: one Sabah bird had especially yellow underparts!
A dark-necked tailorbird found a leafy spot beside a Singapore railway!
The rufous-fronted babbler occurs on the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo.
The rufous-fronted babbler is a little bird, only about 12 cm long!
The rufous-fronted babbler weighs approximately 9–12 grams.
The rufous-fronted babbler has brown plumage and a reddish crown.
The rufous-fronted babbler sings a high-pitched series of repeated notes.
The rufous-fronted babbler favours thick undergrowth and bamboo in open forests and clearings.
The rufous-fronted babbler can be elusive even where the species is common.
The rufous-fronted babbler resembles the rufous-capped babbler in looks and voice, complicating identification where their ranges overlap.
The rufous-fronted babbler may benefit when forest clearance creates suitable scrubby habitat.
The rufous-fronted babbler still has family-life secrets! Most known breeding details come from the Thai-Malay Peninsula.
Short-tailed babblers live across the Malay Peninsula and the islands of Sumatra and Borneo!
The short-tailed babbler measures 13.5–15.5 cm.
Short-tailed babblers have long legs and very short tails.
Adult short-tailed babblers have black moustache-like markings, grey cheek-area feathers and white throats.
Young short-tailed babblers resemble adults but have browner sides to their heads
Short-tailed babblers hunt insects down near the forest floor!
Short-tailed babblers are usually encountered alone or in pairs.
A short-tailed babbler’s song starts with chatter, then about six whistles that drop in pitch!
Short-tailed babbler calls can resemble insects or mechanical sounds.
Short-tailed babblers can live in rainforest that has regrown after earlier disturbance!
Crested honey buzzards have been recorded in many Malaysian places, from Johor to Perlis!
Malay crested honey buzzards breed on the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo.
Crested honey buzzards mainly eat bee and wasp larvae.
Crested honey buzzards’ dense feathers provide partial sting protection.
Crested honey buzzards extract larvae using grooved tongues.
Crested honey buzzards are nearly 60 cm long!
Female crested honey buzzards normally lay two eggs.
Crested honey buzzard parents share chick-raising duties!
Crested honey buzzards have small, pigeon-like heads.
Crested honey buzzards often soar alone or in pairs.
Spotted giant flying squirrels live high in Malaysia’s hills, including Fraser’s Hill!
Spotted giant flying squirrels glide between trees using a skin membrane between their limbs.
Nighttime is activity time for spotted giant flying squirrels!
Spotted giant flying squirrels usually rest in tree hollows during the day.
Spotted giant flying squirrels eat fruits, seeds, leaves, buds and flowers.
Spotted giant flying squirrels in Peninsular Malaysia vary in how heavily their coats are spotted.
Young spotted giant flying squirrels of the northern Bornean form may lack white spots.
Spotted giant flying squirrels usually have one baby per litter, occasionally two.
Acorn-rich oak trees attracted spotted giant flying squirrels at Fraser’s Hill!
Spotted giant flying squirrel head-and-body length is reported as 29.5–40 cm, or up to 36 cm.
Its name says it all, look for those flashy brick-red wing patches against a mostly green body.
You can spot the males by their little maroon "mustache" stripe, the females don't have one.

Mom and dad woodpecker dig out the nest hole together, and they take turns sitting on the 2 to 4 eggs too.

This woodpecker mostly hunts bugs, but it also snacks on figs, and has even been seen sipping nectar straight from flowers!

Rangers patrolling a forest set aside for releasing rescued orangutans spotted this woodpecker too, a good sign the whole forest is healthy.
This woodpecker has been spotted right here in Malaysia, including at Bukit Fraser in Selangor.
The exact type of this bird found in Malaysia also lives across Sumatra, Java, and Borneo, it's a true island-hopper.
Its scientific name literally means "shabby" or "dirty" in Latin, which seems unfair for such a colorful bird!
The Western Hooded Pitta bounces around the forest floor almost like a luminous ball, and despite its bright colors, can be surprisingly difficult to spot in the shaded understory.

Western Hooded Pittas from the Himalayas east through mainland Southeast Asia have a warm brown crown stripe and are migratory, occasionally turning up far outside their normal range, even in city parks.
The Western Hooded Pitta is known for mimicking the calls of other forest birds, which can make identifying it by sound alone especially tricky.
Mom and dad both take turns sitting on the eggs and looking after the chicks once they hatch.
This bird calls out "qweeek-qweeek" over and over to guard its territory, sometimes even all through the night
Instead of building a nest up in a tree, this bird makes its nest right on the forest floor.
Scientists used to think this bird and four of its close species were all the exact same species, until further study split them apart.
In 2010 one of these birds somehow ended up all the way in Australia, thousands of kilometres from home, the first time this species was ever confirmed there.
The Malayan Peacock-Pheasant is one of the shortest-tailed peacock-pheasants, with adult males about 50 cm long, roughly half of that made up by the tail.
When a male wants to impress a mate, the bare skin around his eyes actually changes color, turning bright orange-red.
Most pheasants lay several eggs at once, but this one is known for laying just a single egg.
The male clears a small patch of forest floor as his own personal stage, and calls out from it to stay in touch with his family.
This bird doesn't just show off its feathers, it can actually make clicking, buzzing sounds using its feather quills too!
In just about ten years, two out of every three of these birds disappeared, mostly because the forests they need were cut down.
Nearly all of these birds left in the world now live inside protected Malaysian parks like Taman Negara.
This bird's confirmed sightings in Malaysia are concentrated in just two states, Perak and Selangor.
This bird needs real, untouched forest low in the hills, it almost never lives much higher than 300 metres up.

Almost all of Sarawak's wild orangutans, about 80 percent of them, live in just two protected areas.

This orangutan shares about 97 percent of its DNA with us, we're closer relatives than you might think!
This orangutan actually makes its own umbrella out of leafy branches to stay dry in the rain!
Believe it or not, this mostly fruit-eating ape has sometimes been spotted catching fish with its bare hands.
This orangutan spends more time walking on the ground than its Sumatran cousin does, mostly because Borneo has no tigers to worry about.

Sabah is home to the world's very first official orangutan rescue centre, opened all the way back in 1964.
Between 1985 and 2005, Borneo lost forest the size of a small country every single year, which is a huge reason this orangutan is now critically endangered.
This little monkey lives across most of Peninsular Malaysia, especially in states like Perak and Pahang.

This is the only wild cat tough enough to survive living inside palm oil plantations, mostly because there are so many rats to eat there!
This cat can live almost anywhere, but sadly it's most often spotted crossing roads at night, which puts it at real risk from passing cars.
Researchers have confirmed sightings of this cat in named forest reserves across four different Malaysian states.
The Mainland Leopard Cat's markings vary enough between individuals that researchers can identify specific cats just from their unique spot patterns.
This cat's family tree connects it to some unusual cousins, including the fish-hunting flat-headed cat found in the very same forests.
This cat is doing fine worldwide overall, but in some countries like Nepal, its local population is actually considered at risk.
On one small Singapore island, these cats live in huge numbers, and interestingly, each individual seems to stick to just one type of habitat, either the plantation or the forest, not both.
Long before house cats existed, ancient people in China actually tamed leopard cats first, thousands of years ago!
This cat is such a good swimmer that it has managed to colonize islands off the coast all on its own.

This animal can actually cope living right next to oil palm plantations in parts of Malaysia, not just deep untouched jungle.
Brown Rats can grow to about 28 cm in head-and-body length and weigh around 140–500 g. Their tail is usually shorter than their body.
Their coarse fur is usually brown or brownish-grey above and becomes paler on the belly and chest. Their thick tail is typically darker above and paler below.
Brown Rats are mainly nocturnal, meaning they are most active at night.
They are excellent swimmers and can swim both on the water's surface and underwater.
They are skilled diggers that can create extensive underground burrow systems; in cities, they also use drains and sewers as shelter.
Brown Rats are omnivores and can eat many different foods. Cereals form an important part of their diet, while city rats can survive on discarded human food.
Brown Rats can communicate using ultrasonic sounds that are too high-pitched for humans to hear without special equipment.
Their eyesight is relatively poor, but their eyes can detect ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see.
A female can produce up to about five litters in a year. Pregnancy lasts only around 21 days, and a typical litter contains about seven pups.
Brown Rats are thought to have originated around northern China and neighbouring regions, but they have now spread to every continent except Antarctica.
The Malaysian Field Rat is named after Pulau Tioman, an island off Peninsular Malaysia, and is also commonly called the "Tioman rat."
Its tail is just about as long as the rest of its body put together.
This rat is a great climber and comes out at night, hiding by day in piles of logs or right up inside a palm tree's crown.
This rat has a real taste for oil palm fruit, which is exactly why plantation farmers consider it a pest.
This rat actually evolved resistance to a common rat poison back in the 1980s, forcing plantations to switch to stronger stuff.
If you spot a similar-looking rat, check for an orange spot near the ear, this rat doesn't have one, but a close species  lookalike does.
This little rat has even been found high up on Mount Kinabalu, Malaysia's tallest mountain.
Even though it lives close to farms, this rat almost never sneaks into houses, unlike a lot of its rat relatives.
This rat has confirmed sightings in seven different Malaysian states plus Putrajaya.
By being such easy prey in palm plantations, this rat might actually be helping keep wild leopard cats fed.
This squirrel is a genuine giant, its tail alone can be longer than its whole body, and it's one of the biggest squirrels in the whole region.
The females of this species are actually a bit heavier than the males, even though they're roughly the same length.
Most squirrels sit up straight to eat, but this one hangs sideways off the branch, using its huge tail like a balancing pole.
This squirrel was first officially described on Singapore Island back in 1822, but it hasn't been seen there since 1995, luckily, it still survives in Malaysia.

The very first specimen ever used to officially describe this squirrel has actually gone missing, so scientists in 2026 had to pick a replacement specimen from 1923 to keep the species properly defined.
This squirrel needs real, untouched rainforest to survive, it just can't cope in forests that have been heavily logged.

This bird is so unique it's the only member of its entire genus, it has no close relatives sharing its exact family branch.
The male and female look almost like two different birds, one is glossy black with a wild red mohawk, the other is calm mossy green.
Both male and female Crested Partridges have a bright red ring of bare skin around the eye and red legs without a spur or hind toe.
Its nest isn't up in a tree at all, it's just a hidden dip in the ground, covered over with dead leaves.

If something startles this bird, it usually just runs for cover rather than flying away.
This bird's home stretches from Myanmar all the way to Borneo, living in rainforests up in the hills as well as the lowlands.
Bird watchers in Malaysia know exactly where to look for this bird, the Belum-Temengor forest in the north is a famous spot to find it.
Scientists are still deciding exactly how worried to be about this bird, some call it "near threatened," others call it a step worse, "vulnerable," because logging keeps shrinking its forest home.
This bird weighs about as much as a small bar of soap, and the males are just a bit heavier than the females.
Male Sambar are among the largest deer in Southeast Asia, reaching up to about 1.6 m at the shoulder and around 260 kg.
Only males grow antlers, which usually have three points and can reach about 110 cm long.
Their shaggy coat ranges from yellowish-brown to dark grey, and males usually have a more noticeable dense mane around the neck.
Sambar are mainly active at dusk and during the night, and they are often seen feeding around forest edges.
They eat many kinds of plants, including grasses, leaves, vines, fallen fruits and even water plants.
Adult males usually live alone for much of the year, while females live in small groups; in some places an average group contains only three or four deer.
Sambar are strong swimmers and often gather near water.
When threatened by packs of dogs or dholes, a Sambar may raise its mane, lower its head and strike at the attackers—and it may choose shallow water as a place to defend itself.
When sensing danger, a Sambar can stamp its feet and make a loud ringing alarm call known as “pooking” or “belling.”
Females usually give birth to one calf after a pregnancy of about eight months; the calf begins eating solid food when it is only around 5–14 days old.
This eagle hunts snakes for a living, and its legs are covered in tough, armor-like scales so it doesn't get bitten!
The Crested Serpent Eagle's call has been described as sounding like "iluii..kii-kii-kii-kiiluii," similar to the sound of a bicycle pump.
Unlike most eagles that stay high up, this one has been seen just walking around on the ground at a forest research centre in Selangor!
The Crested Serpent Eagle's species name, "cheela," is derived from the Hindi word for kites, a different group of raptors.
The Crested Serpent Eagle has been officially recorded across every state of Peninsular and East Malaysia, plus the Federal Territory of Putrajaya.
In India these eagles often patch up an old nest to use again, but in Penang, scientists found they build a brand new one every single year.
Small birds called cinereous tits like to build their nests right next to this eagle's nest, using it like a bodyguard against crows!
Snakes and lizards are its favourite meals, but this eagle isn't picky, it'll eat frogs, fish, and even giant earthworms too.
Scientists tracking this eagle found it spends almost the whole day just sitting still, waiting patiently for the right moment to strike.
Mother eagles usually lay just one egg at a time, and it takes almost six weeks to hatch before the chick is finally ready to fly, two months later.
Out of its whole squirrel family group, this one wins for being both the biggest and the most colourful.

Listen for a sharp "CHEK! CHEK!" sound followed by rapid chattering, that's how this squirrel talks to its neighbours.
This squirrel has confirmed sightings on record in two Malaysian states, Johor and Perak.

Even though it isn't endangered yet, this squirrel's numbers could drop if its forest home keeps disappearing.
This pig grows a real beard, and the older it gets, the longer and bushier it grows!
The bearded pigs on the Malaysian Peninsula and the ones in Borneo are actually two different subspecies, you can tell them apart by their coat colour.

Before her piglets are born, a mother bearded pig actually builds a nest out of branches and shrubs, something no other animal in Borneo does.
A mother bearded pig can give birth to as many as 11 piglets at once!

If you spot rounded, symmetric hoofprints in the forest with extra little toe marks, you might be looking at a bearded pig's tracks.

In Malaysia, this pig doesn't just live in the jungle, it also wanders through mangrove swamps, snacking on crabs and shellfish.
The wild boars living in Malaysia are actually smaller than their related species elsewhere in the world, small enough that scientists think they're their own special subspecies.
Mother pigs and their babies like to travel together in a big group, sometimes up to 20 of them, but the fully grown males usually go it alone.
Baby wild boars are born with cute racing stripes down their sides, but those stripes disappear as they grow into adults.
These pigs love a good mud bath, and using the same muddy spot over and over might actually help them get rid of ticks and other pests stuck to their skin.
This pig isn't a picky eater at all, worms, potatoes, fruit, even dead animals are all fair game, and it can live up to 25 years!
A male wild boar's tusks never stop growing throughout its life, and wild boars in cold countries actually grow much bigger than ones living near the equator.
This pig has been officially spotted in states all across Malaysia, from Kedah in the north to Johor in the south.
Nearly every farm pig in the world today can trace its family tree back to wild boars that first appeared right here in Southeast Asia.
This pig's closest living species, the bearded pig, also lives right here on the Malay Peninsula.
This tiny bird has so many nicknames, blue-breasted quail, painted quail, king quail, it's like it can't decide what to be called!

This little bird's family is spread out across an enormous area, from China all the way down to Australia.
Male quails actually battle each other to win the chance to mate, and the winner gets to be extra popular.
Mother quails wait until every single egg is laid before they start sitting on them, then it takes about 16 days for the chicks to hatch.
If this quail gets scared, it shoots straight up into the air, so fast that keepers have to pad the roof of its cage to stop it from bumping its head!
Over a hundred years ago, people tried to bring this quail to New Zealand to live there, but it just didn't work out.
This squirrel belongs to a whole family of striped squirrel cousins across Asia, but the exact kind you'd spot in Malaysia has its own special name, Asiatic Striped Squirrels.
This squirrel used to be considered just a variety of another squirrel, but scientists recently decided it deserves to be called its own species.
Its tail is actually longer than its whole body, and the whole squirrel weighs about as much as a few chocolate bars.
Its back looks like it's wearing a tiny racing jacket, with a black stripe down the middle and pale stripes running alongside it.
This squirrel almost never touches the ground, it spends its whole life up in the trees.
If you visit Fraser's Hill in Malaysia, keep your eyes on the trees, this is one of the places where this squirrel has actually been photographed.
This squirrel usually likes mountain forests high up, but in one part of Thailand it lives right down at sea level among limestone cliffs.

Even scientists are still figuring out exactly how many different kinds of these striped squirrels exist, new DNA studies keep finding more!

This little bird lives across a huge stretch of Asia, from India all the way to the islands of Java and Bali.
This bird is so light it would barely tip a kitchen scale, about as heavy as a few sheets of paper!
It wears a rusty orange cap on its head and a black mask around its eyes, like a tiny masked bandit.
You can tell a male from a female by looking closely at its eyes, males have reddish eyes, females have dark ones.
This bird likes to hide out in tall grass and reeds, not high up in the treetops.

Both mom and dad build the nest together, weaving a little round hut out of dry grass and straw with a doorway on the side.
Its favorite foods are caterpillars and beetles, it's basically a tiny bug hunting machine.

This civet is in serious trouble, more than half its population has disappeared over the last few decades.

This civet's biggest dangers are losing its forest home and getting caught in hunting traps.

This civet is named after Malaysia for a reason, it has been spotted in states all across the country, from Kedah to Sarawak!
This civet is a protected animal in Malaysia, meaning it's against the law to hunt it just for fun.
Flip its tail over and you'll see a totally different pattern, black on top, striped underneath!
It's covered in black spots like a leopard, plus striped collars around its neck!

This civet eats almost anything, bugs, frogs, fruit, even leftover food scraps near villages!
This civet does better in forests that haven't been cut down, mostly because there's more fruit for it to eat there.
Even though this civet is doing okay overall, it can still get caught in ground traps, and some farmers see it as a troublemaker because it raids chicken coops.
This civet is about as long as a golf club from nose to tail, and can weigh as much as a small dog.
This civet isn't just found far away in India, it also roams the forests of Peninsular Malaysia!
You can tell it apart from its cousin, the Malay Civet, just by counting tail rings: this one has far fewer, much bigger black bands!
It has a mohawk-like crest of dark hair running down its back that it can actually raise up!
Around its throat it wears three bold black "necklaces" separated by white bands.
This civet eats a strange mixed menu: fish, frogs, scorpions, and crabs are all on the table!
It leaves smelly "messages" for other civets by marking its territory with scent from special glands.
A large Indian civet can live 15 to 20 years, nearly as long as a family dog!
This civet doesn't just live in lowland jungle, it's been spotted almost 3,000 meters up in the mountains!
Even though this civet is doing fine worldwide, in Singapore it's considered critically endangered, a reminder that local numbers can drop even when the species overall is okay.
It mostly stays on the ground and hunts alone at night, but can climb trees with surprising skill when it needs to!
